#69646. The Open ASR Leaderboard Adds Its First Global South Language

📅 28 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2477 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

The Open ASR Leaderboard Adds Its First Global South Language

📅 28 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voice Arena and Hugging Face partner to launch open ASR evaluation for Hindi and Indian English.
  • A model that scores well on the Open ASR Leaderboard gets adopted and iterated on, while capabilities the leaderboard does not measure tend not to improve.
  • All of that makes one number (WER) harder to game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voice Arena and Hugging Face partner to launch open ASR evaluation for Hindi and Indian English.

Benchmarks decide what gets built. A model that scores well on the Open ASR Leaderboard gets adopted and iterated on, while capabilities the leaderboard does not measure tend not to improve. Much of the recent work on the leaderboard has gone into making the evaluation metrics more trustworthy:.

All of that makes one number (WER) harder to game. It is still one number. A long line of work has shown that ASR error rates are not evenly distributed across the people using them. Racial disparities in automated speech recognition found commercial systems roughly twice as bad for Black speakers as for white speakers, and Quantifying Bias in Automatic Speech Recognition found further differences by gender, age and accent. None of that is visible on a leaderboard, and not because the leaderboard is hiding it. The test sets it runs on record what was said and almost nothing about who said it.

Sources indicate that to address this gap, we introduce two evaluation sets to the Open ASR Leaderboard: Monsoon en-IN and Monsoon hi-IN. Hindi, spoken by more than half a billion people, is the first Indic language on a multilingual tab that currently covers only European languages. Each set is released as a public split, available for self-scoring, and a private split withheld to limit benchmark-specific optimisation. The four splits are speaker-disjoint, comprising 4,888 speakers, with 12 speaker attributes recorded for each.

A test set can only expose a failure mode it varies along. Most benchmarks are built from whatever audio was readily available. Monsoon was built to vary along nine axes: geography, age, gender, vocabulary, devices, acoustic environments, speech type, speech rate, and the existence of multiple valid transcripts for the same audio. Each is a way an aggregate WER can be right on average and wrong for a particular population.

The collection method follows from that.

Four splits, two languages, collected through one pipeline.

The data is sourced from unscripted dual-channel spontaneous conversations, with clips segmented from a single channel so that each clip carries one speaker. Along with the fields reported in the table, each clip also records occupation, education, marital status, income band, handset brand, current city and years in the current district.

Five clips from the public Indian English split, with the metadata each one carries:.

29-year-old woman, West Tripura, Tripura. Student, samsung SM-G781B.

In a recent development, 32-year-old woman, Satna, Madhya Pradesh. Unemployed, samsung SM-E146B.

Industry observers note that 22-year-old man, Rohtas, Bihar. Student, motorola moto g54 5G.

27-year-old woman, Warangal, Telangana. Unemployed, vivo V2247.

57-year-old man, Puducherry. Private job, Xiaomi M2006C3LI.

The English sets use standard string references, where the leaderboard's normaliser collapses most spelling variation. Hindi has far more of it, and no normaliser can resolve it, because the variants are not a fixed mapping between two conventions. The Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, a list of the spellings that are accepted as correct.

Sources indicate that monsoon is small measured in hours and large measured in speakers. That is the design, and it is where most of the value sits.

Speaker concentration and diversity beyond the fields above.

Three properties follow, and each is a claim about variance rather than volume.

Recent findings suggest that no voice carries the score: The ten largest contributors account for between 2.8% and 6.8% of total duration, and more than half of all speakers appear exactly once. A result on Monsoon is an average over hundreds of distinct voices, not a small number of talkers recorded at length. Test sets of comparable duration are usually constructed the other way.

According to recent reports, no region or handset carries it either: The Indian English public set draws on 428 native districts across 30 states and union territories; the Hindi sets, being a Hindi-belt language, concentrate more tightly but still span 202 and 295 districts. Recordings come from 315 to 582 distinct device models, with no single model exceeding 2.1% of segments in any subset. Corpora collected on standardised hardware overfit to one microphone response; this one cannot.

Indian English here is not one accent: This is English as it is spoken across the country, not the English of one region. All six zones are represented: in the public set, 35% of segments are contributed by southern speakers, 18% from the East, 18% from Central, 16% from the North and 11% from the West. The accent variation that follows from that spread is recorded in the metadata rather than asserted.

Monsoon ships 18 columns per segment, of which 12 are metadata, where most public ASR test sets ship an identifier, a transcript and a duration. Demographic fields are complete or near-complete; contributors consented to this use.

The two languages have different geographic shapes, and the shape is informative. The Hindi sets concentrate in the Hindi belt, with Uttar Pradesh accounting for roughly 40% of speakers, which is what a Hindi corpus sampled by population should look like. The Indian English sets are much flatter: no state exceeds 13%, and a third of speakers come from outside the eight largest. Public and private halves match closely on both.

It has been revealed that indian state boundaries were drawn along linguistic lines, so district and state carry real accent signal, which is why these fields are released rather than summarised away. Analysis of this kind has been reported at scale for Indian ASR: district-level error rates spanning roughly 4% to 44%, with underrepresented regions well behind the Hindi belt and the metros, plus disaggregation by audio quality, speaking rate, utterance duration, gender, age and device. Those runs were on a closed benchmark. Monsoon makes the same class of analysis possible on a public leaderboard test set.

Broad geographic coverage requires recruitment across hundreds of districts rather than longer sessions from fewer speakers, and distributed recruitment at this scale introduces failure modes that a smaller collection does not face: contributors gaming the task, played-back audio submitted as live speech, and inattentive annotation. Each is addressed by an explicit check.

Sources indicate that recruitment and recording: Contributors were recruited through the Voice Arena community, a global digital platform whose reach extends into the rural and semi-urban districts that speech corpora rarely cover. Pairs then recorded two-person conversations over a peer-to-peer interface, dual-channel, on assigned everyday topics. Contributors used their own handsets and their own connections. Many of those are low-end devices on unstable bandwidth, which is why that condition is present in the released audio rather than filtered out of it. Prospective contributors completed a language proficiency screening before being granted recording access, were compensated, and provided informed consent covering use in training and distribution. A per-speaker duration cap, calibrated per language to the population size and geographic distribution of its speakers, prevented a small number of prolific contributors from dominating a language or region; more than half of the speakers in these sets contribute exactly one segment.

In a recent development, elicitation: Eliciting spontaneous speech at scale presents its own difficulty, as contributors tend to produce short and sparse responses without structured guidance. Each conversation was therefore seeded with an open-ended narrative cue and progressively revealed follow-up questions, spanning domains including travel, healthcare, agriculture, education and digital services, guiding the exchange toward extended description without scripting it. Candidate topics were generated with large language models, then reviewed and localised by native-speaker linguists.

Quality control: Every recording passed a set of gating checks prior to transcription. The spoken language was verified against the assigned language using language identification models trained on human-annotated data across more than 30 languages. Speaker gender was confirmed against the self-reported label using a dedicated classifier, applied as corroboration of the self-report rather than as a replacement for it. A further model distinguished genuine spontaneous conversation from pre-recorded or played-back audio. Signal-to-noise ratio estimation removed recordings degraded beyond intelligibility, while natural environmental background noise was deliberately preserved so that the acoustic realism of in-the-wild speech is retained. Recordings clearing these checks were segmented by voice activity detection, split at two seconds of continuous silence or at a fifteen-second soft cap closed at the next detected silence. Segmentation was applied independently per channel, so every segment is single-speaker and single-channel. Segments then passed a DNSMOS P.808 check.

In a recent development, transcription: Reference transcripts are human work. A first draft was generated by internal ASR models trained on in-domain data, none of which appear on any public leaderboard, so no system evaluated on these sets contributed to the references it is scored against. Every subsequent stage was performed by native-speaking linguists under a five-level protocol built on a strict separation of labour, in which each correction round is followed by an independent verification round performed by a different annotator, so no linguist audits their own output. A linguist first corrects the draft segment by segment against the acoustic signal; a second re-verifies it and flags residual disagreements. Subsequent levels iterate this cycle with fresh annotators, progressively resolving ambiguous phonetic realisations, code-switching boundaries, named entities, and orthographic consistency across spelling variants. Numerals are written as words, so that the transcript corresponds directly to what was spoken. Segments still flagged at the final level were returned for re-transcription before admission. Annotator behaviour was monitored automatically throughout, flagging submissions containing characters outside the target script, unnatural character or word repetitions, and unusually low or high edit counts.

Recent findings suggest that what follows is one example, run on the public Indian English split, to show the kind of evaluation the metadata makes possible. It is not the finding the sets exist to deliver; it is an illustration of what becomes answerable once every clip carries a speaker.

Sources indicate that eight models on the leaderboard land between 4.81 and 4.99 WER on this set. That is 0.18 points from best to worst, inside what five hours can resolve. Ranked on the corpus, they are the same model.

Industry observers note that grouping speakers by region tells a different story. Each speaker's native district is rolled up to its zonal council, the Ministry of Home Affairs grouping of Indian states, giving five well-sampled zones. openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo varies by 0.46 points across them. mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507, fourteen hundredths of a point behind it on the corpus, varies by 1.68, running 4.38 in the Central zone against 6.06 in the East. Two systems that are indistinguishable on the leaderboard differ almost fourfold in how much their accuracy depends on where the speaker is from.

Which zone is hardest is not fixed either. ibm-granite/granite-speech-3.3-2b is worst in the North, microsoft/VibeVoice-ASR-HF in the South, mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507 in the East. If a single region were simply harder to transcribe, every model would rank the zones the same way. They do not, which points at the models rather than the audio.

Sources indicate that region is one of twelve recorded attributes, and the zones above are a coarse rollup of 428 districts. The same breakdown runs on age, education, occupation and handset, and the released files carry everything needed to reproduce it. None of it is available for a test set that records only what was mentioned.

According to recent reports, english orthographic variation is bounded. British against American spelling, punctuation, casing, digits against words: a normaliser can map most of it to a single form, and the leaderboard's does. Hindi is not bounded in the same way. Everyday speech is heavily code-mixed, English-origin words have no settled Devanagari spelling, and compound forms are written joined or separated according to preference. A single phrase can have ten or more valid written forms, and no fixed mapping collapses them, because there is no canonical side to map to.

According to recent reports, scored with a single reference, WER rewards a system for producing the spelling the annotator happened to choose. Two systems that recognised the audio equally well can differ by several points on orthography alone.

Sources indicate that the Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, the set of written forms accepted as correct. Building it is manual work. Candidate variants are drawn from multiple ASR transcripts of the same audio and expanded with language models, then native-speaker linguists decide which are valid for that utterance and prune the rest, so only forms consistent with what was said are admitted.

It has been revealed that thus, for Hindi we report the Orthographically-Informed Word Error Rate (OIWER), introduced by AI4Bharat, instead of WER. A hypothesis is aligned against the accepted set at each span, so any admitted form counts as correct and only genuine recognition errors are charged.

It has been revealed that to quantify the effect, the same hypotheses were scored twice. Flattening each lattice to its first variant per span yields a single string reference of the kind a conventional benchmark provides; any of the admitted variants would serve equally well, and a different choice would yield a different reference. Scored against the flattened reference, error rates rise for every system, and they do not rise uniformly. Rankings change as a consequence. The figure below demonstrates two pairs of systems that reverse order between the two references: under a single reference a system is rewarded in part for reproducing the annotator's orthography, whereas the lattice scores only recognition.

We also open source our implementation, voi-oiwer, so every result on these sets can be reproduced directly.

Recent findings suggest that for the private splits, get your model on the Open ASR Leaderboard and the Hugging Face team will run the evaluation. As before, the process for adding a model to the leaderboard takes place on the Open ASR Leaderboard GitHub:.

Indian-English joins the main leaderboard as Voice Arena Monsoon, in the default column set rather than as an opt-in toggle, so it contributes to the headline Average WER for every model. The private split feeds the aggregated Private (conversational) column alongside Appen and DataoceanAI data. The public and private Hindi appears in the Multilingual tab, where a model is ranked only if it supports every selected language, making that column a like-for-like comparison. Alternative, select "Hindi" from the "Language dataset breakdown" dropdown menu.

Hindi is a sharp case of a general problem. Any language written more than one way, spoken by people a benchmark has not sampled, carries both of the failures described here. These sets do not fix them. What they add is a way to see them: a test set on a leaderboard the field already watches, carrying enough about each speaker and each reference that a difference between two systems can be traced to who was talking and how they write it, instead of disappearing into one number.

These four sets are part of Monsoon, Voice Arena's broader dataset initiative for the Global South.

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities.
  • In a recent development, using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process.
  • In a recent development, continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting concerns by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

In a recent development, using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

In a recent development, continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting matter by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

According to recent reports, continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

Sources indicate that for each confirmed concern, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

Industry observers note that AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review challenges, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

I open one of my environments. The Issues tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

Sources indicate that the Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other users in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

Recent findings suggest that the Remediation section highlights a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that issues are built from.

The Scans tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

In a single workflow, I work through the validated issues in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

Sources indicate that now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page.

According to recent reports, to learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#69644. Industry News: Coding Agent Horror Stories: The CVE That Did Not Exist

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2962 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Docker ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Coding Agent Horror Stories: The CVE That Did Not Exist

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is Part 6 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line.
  • Every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched.
  • The agent in this one reached nothing at all, because it was deliberately built so that it could not.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Part 6 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line.

Every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched. We have seen agents wander into home directories, drop production databases, leak credentials, and run shell commands that did something very different from what the developer expected. In each case, the damage came from the agent having more reach than it needed.

This story is the opposite. The agent in this one reached nothing at all, because it was deliberately built so that it could not. And yet, on the night in question, it was still the most dangerous thing in the pipeline.

This story was shared by Pratik Kumar Singh as part of our Agent Hall of Shame contest on social media.

In a recent development, A platform engineer built a code review bot for his team. The idea was simple and useful. Every time someone pushes code, the bot reads what changed and writes a review into the pipeline, the same kind of first pass a human teammate would give before a person looks at the change.

According to recent reports, he named the bot BuaJi. In India, your bua is your father’s sister, and in many families she is the relative who inspects everything you do and always manages to find something wrong with it. For a code reviewer, it is a fitting name.

Sources indicate that what made BuaJi interesting was how carefully it was set up. The bot runs on local models through Ollama, which means the model weights sit on the engineer’s own hardware and no request ever goes out to an AI vendor. It also runs as a job in his CI pipeline, triggered whenever someone pushes code. Taken together, this makes the whole setup self-hosted. The code it reads is tech giant source code, and with this design none of it ever leaves the building. That was a deliberate choice, because his company takes that seriously.

He also gave BuaJi one firm rule: it can read, and it can comment, and that is all. It cannot run terraform apply, which is the command that creates or changes real cloud infrastructure. It cannot run kubectl apply, which changes what is actually running in the Kubernetes cluster. And it cannot push a commit, so it has no way to change the code itself. Those are the commands that change the real world, and BuaJi was given none of them. On paper, this is exactly how you would want an AI reviewer to be built.

The version of BuaJi in the companion repo is a deliberately minimal reviewer. It checks Go files against a handful of style rules. The report below is the kind of free-form finding any reviewer produces once you let it comment in prose rather than pass/fail, which is exactly the direction these bots get pushed in practice.

Industry observers note that his product ships with a bundled copy of PostgreSQL. Older PostgreSQL releases have published vulnerabilities with CVE numbers attached, and upgrading to a newer patch release is how you make those known problems go away. So he bumped the version.

In a recent development, this is about as boring and as responsible as a code change gets. It touches a few lines, it changes a version number, and its only purpose is to close security holes that are already public. Any reviewer, human or machine, should look at it and approve it in a few seconds. There is nothing in that diff to be suspicious about, and that is precisely why what happened next matters.

According to recent reports, buaJi responded with roughly fifteen hundred words rejecting the change. For context, a normal review comment is a sentence or two.

It has been revealed that the report described the version bump as an “architectural takeover,” a structural change smuggled into the codebase under the cover of routine maintenance. It claimed that the latest PostgreSQL build was a vehicle for sending internal data to a third-party company, and it named that company outright. The company does not exist.

It went further. It referred to specific Kubernetes resources by name, as though it had inspected the cluster and found them. Those resources had never existed, and BuaJi had no access to the cluster that would have let it look. It then wrote Go scripts to “isolate the infected PostgreSQL nodes,” even though nothing was infected. Finally, it told the engineer to revoke all IAM access immediately, an action that would lock out every person in the organization, including the people who would be needed to fix any real problem.

Holding the whole argument together was a CVE number that has never been issued by anyone. Of everything in the report, this is the detail worth pausing on. A CVE identifier is one of the easiest things in security to verify, since you can look it up in a public registry in a few seconds. The bot invented a fact in the one place where invented facts are easiest to catch.

And yet the report looked completely convincing. The Markdown was clean and well structured. The YAML it proposed would have parsed without errors. The tone was urgent and confident, the way a senior security engineer writes when they have found something serious and need you to act before it gets worse. The engineer spent about two minutes reading the CI logs, realized that none of it was real, and went back to what he was doing.

Caption: Comic illustrating how a confident, well-formatted security report from an AI reviewer can be entirely fabricated, and what happens when somebody acts on it.

It is important to say clearly that the read-only rule did its job. BuaJi could not carry out any of its own recommendations, and it never had any access to the cluster. Because of that, the entire episode cost the engineer two minutes of his evening and nothing more.

It has been revealed that the trouble is that the rule only controlled what BuaJi could do. Nobody had thought about what BuaJi could say. A read-only agent is still allowed to tell people what to do, and the person reading its output usually has exactly the access that the agent was denied. BuaJi could not run the scripts it wrote, but it could write them down and hand them to someone who could.

This engineer caught the problem because he knows his own cluster well. He knew those Kubernetes resources were not real and that nothing had been compromised. Now imagine a newer engineer on call at two in the morning, half awake, looking at a long and alarming security report in the pipeline. Revoking all IAM access in production in the middle of the night is an outage all by itself. Running an unreviewed Go script against your database nodes could be considerably worse. In both scenarios, BuaJi would not have done anything. A person would have done all of it, in good faith, because the report told them to.

Sources indicate that what makes this so hard to defend against is that no permission model would have flagged it, because no permission was ever violated. The agent stayed within its boundary. The engineer had every right to run those commands on his own systems. The only thing in the entire chain that was false was the content of the report.

Here’s the honest part: a sandbox is not a fact-checker. No microVM boundary will ever make a review comment accurate. What a boundary changes is what that fabricated output can do once it exists.

In a recent development, remember where BuaJi’s read-only rule actually lived, in a convention. One engineer configured it in his own pipeline and has to keep remembering to leave it in place. Rules like that hold until someone is in a hurry, or a latest teammate copies the config and drops a section they did not understand, or a small exception made for a good reason quietly becomes permanent. None of this needs bad intent; it is just how real teams work.

Docker Sandboxes run agents inside isolated microVMs each with its own kernel, its own filesystem, and a network that denies everything by default. An agent inside one can invent anything it likes, but the invention has nowhere to go: no credentials to use, no cluster to reach, no commit to push, unless someone allowed that access ahead of time. The read-only rule stops being something a person remembers and becomes a property of the environment. And when a report claims it inspected your cluster, the policy log is your proof it never could have.

That protects you from the agent. It does nothing for the human who reads the output, and no sandbox ever will. For that half, treat agent review output the way you already treat agent input, untrusted until something checks it: label it so it doesn’t carry a colleague’s weight, verify any CVE numbers, and never run agent-written remediation until a person has read and understood it.

Industry observers note that this is the same pattern as the sandbox escapes Pillar published in July. The boundary itself was never broken; a file was written inside the sandbox, and a tool outside later trusted it. An agent’s output is always an input to whatever reads it next and somewhere downstream, something trusts what it receives. Very often, that something is a person.

It has been revealed that let’s move BuaJi into a Docker Sandbox, one step at a time. By the end, the read-only rule is enforced by the environment, not by memory.

BuaJi is a small Python script, buaji.py. Its GitLab job installs Ollama on a GPU runner, starts ollama serve, loads the model named in LLM, and runs the script.

Industry observers note that the script reads review rules from rules.md and finds the changed files with git diff HEAD^ HEAD --name-only. It sends each file and rule to Ollama at http://localhost:11434 and prints the answers to the CI log.

Industry observers note that the catch is that everything shares one container: the model, the script, the checkout and every CI variable, including CI_JOB_TOKEN. BuaJi is read-only only because the script happens not to write anything.

According to recent reports, we split the job in two. The model stays on the runner next to the GPU. BuaJi moves into a microVM that can read the code, talk to the model, and nothing else.

One open path to the model, everything else blocked, and a CVE check on the way out.

It has been revealed that inside a sandbox, localhost is the sandbox itself. So we read the Ollama address from an environment variable and keep the old value as the default:.

Outside a sandbox, nothing changes. Inside one, we point OLLAMA_URL at the runner.

Today the job runs apt-get and pip3 install on every run, which needs internet access each time.

Instead, build a small image once with everything BuaJi needs, so the sandbox never downloads anything:.

Push it to your registry and store its name in a CI variable called BUAJI_TEMPLATE.

According to recent reports, ollama stays on the runner with the GPU. Install it once on the runner instead of running curl | sh in every pipeline.

The model never enters the sandbox. BuaJi reaches it through one port, opened in Step 5.

This step decides what BuaJi can see and change.

Notice what is missing: no GitLab token, no kubeconfig, no cloud credentials. Even if BuaJi tried kubectl or terraform, it would have nothing to connect with.

Recent findings suggest that sandboxes block all outgoing traffic by default. We open one path, for this sandbox only. (This assumes the runner’s default policy is deny-all; on a balanced or open default, set the default to deny-all first.).

The allow target (localhost:11434) and the address BuaJi dials (host.docker.internal:11434) are two names for the same runner port,  the first from the runner’s point of view, the second from inside the microVM. Kubernetes, your cloud APIs, and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

Kubernetes, your cloud APIs and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

BuaJi runs as before, just in a latest place with only two variables:.

The review is now just text. BuaJi cannot post it, act on it, or change what happens to it next.

Sources indicate that this check would have caught the fake report in seconds. It runs on the runner, so BuaJi cannot skip it.

It looks up every CVE ID in the NVD database and fails the job if any of them do not exist:.

According to recent reports, because the job is allow_failure: true, GitLab marks it “passed with warnings.” The pipeline keeps moving, but nobody mistakes the report for a trusted one. This degrades the signal, it does not block the human. The warning is a nudge, not a guardrail ~ a tired on-call engineer can still scroll past it..

Industry observers note that it won’t catch every made-up detail, like a fake Kubernetes resource name. But it catches the one that holds most fake reports together.

Finally, review the policy log and remove the sandbox:.

Industry observers note that the log shows every host BuaJi tried to reach. On a deny-all runner, a healthy run shows only the model on port 11434. Anything else is a signal worth looking at.

Removing the sandbox means every pipeline starts clean.

Put together, the buaji job in .gitlab-ci.yml looks like this:.

Recent findings suggest that the runner needs a GPU and KVM, which usually means self-hosted. GIT_DEPTH: "2" gives buaji.py the two commits it compares. The cleanup sits in after_script, so it runs even when the job fails.

Before, the read-only rule lived in the script. Now it lives in the environment: a read-only checkout, one network path, no credentials, and only checked text coming out.

What hasn’t changed is the human reading the output. The sandbox stops BuaJi from running its scripts. Only the CVE check and a careful reader stop someone else from running them.

In a recent development, treat an agent’s security finding as a hypothesis, not a conclusion. A report from an AI reviewer is a claim with good formatting. When a human reviewer flags a security issue, there is an implied step where they checked their reasoning. With an agent, that step has not happened, so you have to do it yourself.

Verify every CVE number before acting on it. This is the cheapest check in the whole process and it catches the single most convincing part of a fabricated report. Automate it, as in Step 7, so it runs on every review without anyone having to remember.

Never run agent-written remediation without reviewing it first. Scripts and commands supplied by an agent are the point where a false finding turns into a real incident. Read them with the same care you would give an unknown script from the internet.

Make read-only a property of the environment, not a habit. A restriction you enforce by hand in a pipeline config is always one rushed change away from disappearing. Mount the code read-only, pass in no credentials, and open only the network paths the agent needs, as in Steps 4 to 6.

It has been revealed that clearly label agent review output as agent output. When a bot’s review looks identical to one from a senior engineer, it borrows authority it has not earned. A clear label helps readers apply the right level of skepticism.

Keep an eye on your signal-to-noise ratio. The curl story is the warning here. A review channel that fills up with noise eventually stops being read, and a review channel nobody reads is worse than having none, because people still assume it is protecting them.

The engineer who built BuaJi was right that the read-only rule protected him, and it genuinely did. BuaJi could not touch the cluster, could not revoke anyone’s access, and could not run a single line of the code it had so carefully written. What the rule could not do was stop BuaJi from asking somebody else to run it.

Every other story in this series has been about an agent reaching too far. This one never reached at all. It stayed inside its boundary, did exactly what it was permitted to do, and still produced a document that would have caused a real outage if the person reading it had been a little more tired, or a little less familiar with their own cluster.

As we give agents more responsibility in our pipelines, containing what they can do is only half the job. A sandbox handles that half. The other half is deciding how much we trust what they tell us, and that part is still up to us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ransomware group sets a deadline for the chipmaker to pay up - or see its data leaked.

In a recent development, finding a new CEO is just one of their problems. Nvidia is investigating an alleged breach following claims by ransomware group The Gentlemen's affiliates that they hacked the AI giant and stole sensitive information.

The embattled chipmaker told The Register's that it was investigating a possible third-party data breach. “We have found no indication that Nvidia systems or networks were affected,” a spokesperson said. “We continue to monitor the situation.".

The ransomware gang’s data-leak site, shared on social media and seen by The Register, doesn’t show any stolen files or indicate what information the group claims to have stolen. Nvidia first appeared on the criminals’ blog on Wednesday, with The Gentlemen promising “DATA INFO - SOON.”.

The post also included a countdown, ending November 28.

While we can’t verify the criminals’ claims, the group, which emerged in mid-2025, is one of the most prolific ransomware-as-a-service operations. Its affiliates claimed more than 320 victims as of April, with the majority of these alleged ransomware infections (240) occurring in the first half of 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the actual count, however, is likely much higher. Check Point researchers accessed an affiliate’s live command-and-control server during an incident response case earlier this year. The server contained victim telemetry that revealed more than 1,570 victims, mostly located in the US, and primarily corporate and organizational environments.

According to an operational technology (OT) threat report from Trellix published on Wednesday, industrial ransomware claims jumped nearly 51 percent - to about 1,500 posts- compared to last quarter, and The Gentlemen’s affiliates were the most prolific claim posters during this time period. They accounted for about 16 percent of all posts.

Industry observers note that in February 2022, an Nvidia data breach exposed employees’ credentials and proprietary code. Extortion crew Lapsus$ claimed to be responsible for that intrusion and data theft.®.

#69642. Latest Update: Introducing @huggingface/kernels: 200+ WebGPU Kernels for Local AI

📅 01 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1606 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Introducing @huggingface/kernels: 200+ WebGPU Kernels for Local AI

📅 01 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, one of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible.
  • Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels, a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels.
  • The collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible. Getting there is a multi-layer effort: models need browser-friendly representations, runtimes need to build efficient execution looks, and the individual GPU operations at the bottom of the stack need to make the most of many different devices and browser implementations.

Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels, a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels.

The collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads. More importantly, each kernel is published as a complete, versioned package: its interface, shader templates, correctness cases, benchmark cases, and usage instructions all live together on the Hub.

According to recent reports, we are also launching Fleet, an in-browser GPU benchmarking and testing suite that runs and scores the kernels on your hardware. Beyond the results for your own machine, Fleet gives the community a way to contribute performance and correctness evidence from devices we could never cover in a conventional test lab. With your consent, every run adds private evidence that can help us find failures (incorrect results, pathologically slow cases, etc.), improve kernel variants, and make better optimization decisions across real-world hardware.

A model running in the browser eventually becomes a sequence of GPU operations: matrix multiplications, normalizations, convolutions, attention primitives, quantization operations, data-layout transformations, and many more. WebGPU makes these operations available across modern browsers through a portable API, while WGSL provides a common language for the shaders that execute them.

Industry observers note that portability, however, does not automatically mean performance. Two shaders can implement the same operation and produce the same output while behaving completely differently across different accelerators. Workgroup sizes, memory access patterns, vectorization, data types, and fusion strategies can all affect performance. The best choice can also change with the input shape, device, browser, and available WebGPU features.

Sources indicate that this is why kernels form a foundational layer of fast browser inference. Higher-level runtimes can only be as efficient as the operations they dispatch. By making those operations individually discoverable, testable, benchmarkable, and versioned, we can improve the foundation independently while keeping a stable contract for the layers above it.

Each kernel in the collection has its own repository and kernel card. The card documents the operation's semantics, inputs, outputs, attributes, supported data types, source files, and a ready-to-run @huggingface/kernels example.

For example, ai.onnx.Add implements elementwise addition with multidirectional broadcasting. It is one of the simplest operations in a neural network, used everywhere from residual connections to adding a bias. Its card documents the two inputs, the broadcasted output shape, supported data types, and the variants available for different shapes and devices.

Behind the card, the repository contains the artifacts needed to understand and evaluate the implementation:.

According to recent reports, this structure turns a shader into a reusable software artifact. The interface is inspectable without reading WGSL, correctness and performance cases travel with the implementation, and published versions can be loaded explicitly rather than depending on an unversioned file URL. Our kernels can also serve as reference implementations for developers building custom WebGPU kernels or integrating these operations into their own runtimes.

According to recent reports, running these kernels requires a browser with WebGPU support. WebGPU availability depends on the browser, operating system, GPU, and driver. You can check for it in JavaScript with "gpu" in navigator.

In a recent development, @huggingface/kernels provides the bridge between a kernel repository and your application. Call getKernel with a Hub repository ID and a contract version, then invoke the returned function with typed input data and tensor shapes. Here is a small bias-add example:.

The second input is broadcast across the first dimension, producing an output with shape [2, 3]. The loader derives that output shape and logical data type from the manifest contract and the inputs, then allocates c automatically.

Industry observers note that addition on six floats is deliberately the smallest possible demo. At this size, the GPU round trip costs far more than the math. The point is the call pattern: it stays exactly the same for the heavyweight operations where optimized kernels actually pay off, such as matrix multiplication (ai.onnx.MatMul). Only the repository ID and the inputs change.

Even this elementary operation illustrates why kernels need variants. Equal-shape addition can use a direct vectorized path, while broadcasted inputs need different indexing logic. The published Add kernel includes variants for equal shapes, vectorized broadcasting, scalar processing, and general broadcasting. The runtime can select an implementation that fits the current call and device without changing the application-facing API.

Sources indicate that the version: 1 option selects version 1 of the published kernel contract. It is separate from an ONNX opset, an operator's since_version, or a model revision. Keeping those concepts separate lets applications depend on a stable JavaScript-facing contract while kernel implementations evolve behind it.

So, how much of a difference do optimized kernels actually make? We put our collection head-to-head with ORT WebGPU on an Apple M4 GPU, using ONNX Runtime Web 1.30.0-dev.20260826-b1f76d586a. We started with 1,756 test cases across all 207 operations and kept the 809 cases where both sides produced matching outputs and reliable timings.

According to recent reports, across those comparisons, our kernels were 2.57x faster by geometric mean and 1.90x faster at the median, with 629 wins, 176 losses, and 4 ties. Here is a closer look at four familiar operations:.

Some individual wins were much bigger. A particularly difficult bilinear Einsum case (i,ij,j with size 4096) ran in 0.136 ms with our kernel versus 1,396 ms with ORT WebGPU: more than 10,000x faster. A row-wise CumSum over [256, 4096] was 301x faster, at 0.016 ms versus 4.784 ms. These are unusual cases rather than the speedups you should expect everywhere, but they show how much a specialized kernel can help when a general implementation hits a slow path.

We timed the work done on the GPU itself, leaving out setup such as loading kernels, creating sessions, uploading inputs, compiling shaders, and reading outputs back. Very short workloads are naturally harder to measure, and small cases can benefit from the GPU cache, so these numbers are best read as a useful comparison rather than a promise for every application.

According to recent reports, they are also results for individual operations, not complete models. Exact performance will change across GPUs and browsers, which is why Fleet is so vital for building a broader picture.

We are also working with the ONNX Runtime team to upstream these improvements so they can benefit the broader ONNX Runtime Web ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that webGPU performance varies across GPUs, browsers, and drivers, so results from one machine only tell part of the story. Fleet lets anyone run correctness and performance checks in the browser and see how the kernels behave on their hardware.

Recent findings suggest that with consent, each run privately contributes evidence that helps us spot device-specific failures, compare variants, and improve selection rules. The goal is simple: use broad, real-world coverage to make the kernels faster and more reliable for everyone.

Industry observers note that the initial 207 kernels are a starting point, not the end state. Publishing kernels independently on the Hub gives us a common place to inspect contracts, compare implementations, reproduce correctness checks, and improve performance without embedding every shader directly into every runtime.

The collection is also part of the Hub's broader kernel ecosystem: on the Kernels page, the WebGPU kernels sit alongside kernels for CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and other platforms, and can be filtered, sorted, and explored like any other artifact on the Hub.

The pieces reinforce one another:.

Recent findings suggest that this is the low-level foundation for the next steps in our browser inference stack. We are excited to connect these kernels to higher-level model tooling, continue expanding operation coverage, and make fast local inference easier to use across the WebAI ecosystem.

Explore the WebGPU kernel collection, try @huggingface/kernels, and join the Fleet to contribute evidence from your device and help us make the kernels better for everyone.

The Fleet part may matter as much as the kernels. The 809 comparable cases on an M4 are useful, but browser, driver and device variance is where WebGPU tends to get painful. Will Fleet eventually expose per-device distributions, or is the blueprint to use the runs only for aggregate selection rules?

In an automated build system, I could see per device kernels, made more interesting by fusion of ops.

The area that obviously needs more attention are the 947 tests that did not result in reliable output. This could be the test, it could be that the ORT WebGPU is wrong, or the upcoming kernel is wrong, or the test harness had issues, hard to know from the outside. Perhaps the Fleet thing is meant to improve this.

Very excited to see such attention at making WebGPU first class in ML!

Industry observers note that @sroussey Agreed—the excluded 947 need a taxonomy before the 2.57× summary can travel. I'd want counts by operation and device for unsupported, ORT mismatch, newly introduced-kernel mismatch, and harness/timeout, with raw failing cases downloadable. Then Fleet can optimize only within a proven-correct compatibility envelope; fusion and per-device tuning become much safer.

It has been revealed that excellent! This will help our WebAI community continue developing highly optimized solutions. Many thanks @Xenova and @nico-martin for the great work you have been doing.

Where should your code live in a Docker Sandbox?

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1197 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on.
  • You might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results.
  • According to recent reports, sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on. You can share a checkout from your host, give it a separate working directory for a task, or keep the repository entirely inside the sandbox. Each arrangement changes how you, the human, participate in the work.

You might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results. sbx supports both. The way you organize the checkout can change as you ask the agent to take on more of the work.

According to recent reports, sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use. Run sbx run from your project directory, and it mounts that directory at the same absolute path inside the sandbox:.

It has been revealed that open a file in your local editor while the agent works on it, and you’ll see changes as they happen. Git works from either side, so you choose whether you want to let the agent make commits or you do it yourself. Development servers on your host can pick up the edits through hot reload, using the runtime and dependencies installed on your host.

This fits close collaboration on one task. The coordination cost comes from sharing that working tree: switching branches changes the files the agent sees, and your edits become part of its ongoing work. If you want to switch to something unrelated while the agent continues, you’ll need another checkout.

Industry observers note that NOTE: Dependencies written into the shared checkout are shared too. Packages with native binaries, such as esbuild, may work in the Linux sandbox and fail on a macOS or Windows host. Reinstalling on the host can reverse the problem. Keep separate dependency installations, or run the app consistently in one environment.

Git worktrees give each task a directory and branch. You can mount each worktree in its own sandbox, while your original checkout remains available for other work. The agent’s edits appear in the worktree. You can inspect either with your local editor and development tools. Each task also gets its own running environment, with tools to prepare and a sandbox and worktree to clean up afterward.

It has been revealed that there is a Git limitation with mounting only a linked worktree. Its .git file points to metadata outside the mount, which the agent can’t reach. It can edit files, but checking status, branching, and committing have to happen on the host. The future of software development still needs you to run git status.

sbx supports a clone mode that gives the agent a separate checkout with Git available inside the sandbox. You keep your local project, but sbx mounts the host source as read-only and creates an independent clone for the agent. Its branch changes and dependency installations stay in its checkout.

Bringing the result back becomes a handoff. While the sandbox is running, you can fetch committed branches through the Git remote sbx adds on your host. Or the agent can push to the repository’s remote and you can retrieve the branch through your usual Git workflow. Your local editor and development server see the changes after you bring them into your checkout.

In a recent development, A mountless sandbox has no host workspace directory attached. Clone the repository inside it, and the sandbox holds the checkout and its development environment. Your host copy of the project shares no connection with the sandbox checkout.

This workflow resembles working on a remote development machine. Agents connect to the project environment, and you can open a shell with sbx exec or connect an editor to the sandbox over SSH. Changes and dependency installations stay separate from your host. To bring work back, you push a branch to the Git remote.

It has been revealed that one sandbox per project can be a useful mental model here. The project and its tools persist across agent sessions and sandbox restarts. An agent can create worktrees per feature it’s working on, push branches, and create pull requests for review. Starting another task doesn’t require you to prepare another host worktree and sandbox, and the agent has Git access in each working directory. Clone mode supports this internal-worktree approach too.

Those tasks share tools and services, so running servers or changing the environment still needs coordination. Separate sandboxes are useful when tasks need independent environments as well as separate files. Branches alone don’t isolate simultaneous edits in one working directory.

Industry observers note that that independence adds some distance when you want to try the result. Your usual local editor isn’t looking at these files, and a development server running inside the sandbox needs a published port to reach it from your browser.

For a web app preview, ask the agent:.

Start the development server on port 8080, bound to 0.0.0.0.

Then publish the port from another terminal on the host:.

It has been revealed that open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. It’s possible to work interactively this way, but there’s more ceremony than opening a project already on your filesystem.

An environment file can make setup repeatable, selecting tools and cloning the repository at creation with something like the community github-clone kit. Recreating the sandbox then gives you a fresh environment. Push or copy out work you want to retain first: removing a sandbox deletes files held only there.

An API change might need a corresponding frontend change, or another repository might provide useful reference material. You can mount several directories into one sandbox, with read-only access for reference repositories. Local editing and previews remain available, but each writable checkout needs branch and change coordination. Task-specific checkouts also leave directories to clean up afterward.

Sources indicate that A workspace manager such as jganoff/wsp can assemble selected repositories for a task. Mounting that workspace gives the agent the projects it needs together. These are standard clones with their own Git metadata, so the agent retains Git access, unlike a mounted linked worktree.

The same scope fits inside a mountless sandbox: clone the repositories needed there and keep the whole workspace in the sandbox. The number of repositories and where their files live are separate choices.

The checkout’s location, the sandbox’s lifetime, and the repositories it contains are choices you can combine. You can keep a project sandbox around for many tasks, or mount a workspace assembled for one job. What suits you may change when you want to work more closely with the agent, or give it more room to manage the work itself.

The Git workflows documentation covers the mechanics of direct mounts, clone mode, and host worktrees.

Docker publishes fixed images for both Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 latest voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice.

Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.

Sources indicate that the rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

According to recent reports, AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks problems by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation presently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future.

In a recent development, the “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon).

Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer.

The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge.

Last week’s debuts Here are some launches that caught my attention this week.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 fresh voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural.

AWS announces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta) – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the AWS Insights piece on that theme is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside AWS Neuron 2.33.

New ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a full technical walkthrough, the training session APIs, and new support for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3.

Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate.

Recent findings suggest that amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools. It is available in all commercial Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Other AWS news Here are some additional projects and posts that you might find interesting.

Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry – AWS Agent Registry is a managed catalog for MCP servers, agents, and agent skills, so an orchestrator can search approved capabilities at runtime instead of compiling every tool in at build time. This walkthrough reveals the discover, instantiate, and execute loop in a working sample, with search results that return connection metadata but never invocation credentials.

Tokenomics for coding agents: benchmark cost and quality on your own code – Coding assistants replay a growing transcript on every turn, so their cost math is nothing like ordinary inference. This post gives you open source tooling to measure model, harness, and hosting choices on your own repositories and build a cost-and-quality frontier you own, with sample results where routing came out 44.7 percent cheaper for 4.8 percent lower mean quality.

In a recent development, how U.S. Bank migrated 119 TB from Oracle Exadata to Amazon RDS for Oracle – U.S. Bank moved four Oracle Exadata databases totaling about 119 TB to Amazon RDS for Oracle using a config-driven pipeline built on Oracle XTTS, AWS DataSync, and Amazon EFS. The initial baseline copy finished in about 7 days with zero data loss and cutovers averaging roughly four hours per database, over a bandwidth-capped Direct Connect link.

Upcoming AWS events Mark your calendars for these upcoming events.

Sources indicate that AWS re:Invent – AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, with more than 2,200 sessions. The session catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so now is the time to build your schedule.

AWS Community Days – AWS Community Day Brasil Norte takes place in Belém on October 31, closing out the 2026 Brazilian community season. Check the hub for events near you.

Security shop buys the hand that feeds it.

As AI has become a thorn in the side of the security industry, Palo Alto Networks (PAN) has reached an agreement to acquire Applied Compute, an AI model training platform.

It has been revealed that "We believe many of the major disruptions of the last few weeks, including outages across major enterprises and governments, were partially due to unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes, as IT teams simply cannot patch these vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising their production environments," mentioned Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, during the tech giant's fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Wednesday. "The second effect is the rise of AI-assisted cyberattacks.".

It has been revealed that so in the spirit of "hair of the dog that bit me," PAN is ingesting Applied Compute to make open-weight AI more secure for corporate customers. The answer to insecurity brought on by AI is buying security with AI.

In its announcement of the tie-up, PAN declares "the future of enterprise AI is hybrid, and that a large share of enterprises will run on open-source and open-weight models tuned to their own data, cost, and control needs.".

That view has been clouded a bit by Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's fall from grace: Back in July, he came to the defense of open-weight models as a defense against the hegemony of purveyors of closed-weight commercial models like Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. His resignation as CEO of Nvidia has led to worries that the open-weight ecosystem has lost some lobbying power at a time when the US is wary about the uptake of models made in China.

Nonetheless, PAN clearly sees a future for open-weight models.

"Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, in a statement. "Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we've seen, and its research team is exceptional.".

The company expects the $4.5 billion all-stock transaction to add more than $1 billion to the company's Next Generation Security business by FY 2029.

Arora, on the organization's earnings call, explained the pricey bet as recognition of the corporate desire to avoid vendor lock-in and to retain control of data.

"We're already seeing the desire for sovereignty and control compel enterprises to adopt open-weight and open-source models," he noted. "Early signs of that shift are clear, with open-weight models growing from under 5 percent of token traffic to more than 60 percent over the past year.".

Sources indicate that beyond the sticker price, PAN is ready to up its infrastructure ante. Arora said the biz expects to build infrastructure supporting more than 100 megawatts of inference capacity, a project that will take "a modest CapEx commitment of less than $3 billion through fiscal 2030." ®.

#69637. BenchMIRT: What are LLM benchmarks actually measuring?

📅 01 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1393 w)
