  • We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

Recent findings suggest that modernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

It has been revealed that neoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

In a recent development, neoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

In a recent development, we pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Industry observers note that pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

Sources indicate that we report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

In a recent development, † Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

People can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Industry observers note that before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

According to recent reports, so we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers right now supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

It has been revealed that visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Organization for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A coding agent in Docker Sandboxes runs inside an isolated VM, the sandbox controls which hosts it can reach, and credentials stay on the host behind a proxy.
  • The Firecrawl kit gives the agent web search, page scraping, and site crawling through one added host, api.firecrawl.dev, and every page comes back as clean markdown.
  • The Firecrawl kit is a mixin (kind: mixin): it extends whichever workload you already run rather than defining a new sandbox.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A coding agent in Docker Sandboxes runs inside an isolated VM, the sandbox controls which hosts it can reach, and credentials stay on the host behind a proxy. The same controls keep the agent from opening a docs page, reading a changelog, or looking up an API that shipped after its training cutoff, so it writes code against the version it remembers. The usual fix is to widen the allowlist until the agent can fetch anything, which hands back most of what the sandbox took away.

The Firecrawl kit gives the agent web search, page scraping, and site crawling through one added host, api.firecrawl.dev, and every page comes back as clean markdown.

The Firecrawl kit is a mixin (kind: mixin): it extends whichever workload you already run rather than defining a new sandbox. Its descriptor, firecrawl/firecrawl.yaml, declares four typed capabilities:.

Industry observers note that the kit adds to the sandbox’s allowlist and does not narrow it, so everything else is set by your global sbx policy. Docker’s balanced preset allows package registries, GitHub, and a curated list of vendor domains, and returns a 403 for general websites, including most documentation sites, so Firecrawl is the agent’s route to those. Under deny-all, it is the agent’s only web host.

Sources indicate that kits are experimental and in Early Access, so the kit format and sbx commands may change. The steps below are current for October 2026; the repository README carries the latest.

Sources indicate that kit: docker.io/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl:1.0.0 on Docker Hub, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. Source: github.com/firecrawl/firecrawl-docker-sandbox.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Store the key once on the host. The command prompts for the key. Service secrets are global by default, so every sandbox that requests the firecrawl service can use it once you approve. The kit never sees the value; the proxy injects it at request time.

Sources indicate that 2. Start a sandbox with the kit. The kit is an ordinary OCI image with its descriptor in the manifest, so a version tag is all you need. Each --kit adds a mixin to the workload, and the trailing . mounts your project directory.

On the first run, sbx asks you to approve sending the firecrawl credential to api.firecrawl.dev. Accept the defaults. The credential is required: with no secret stored, sbx refuses to create the sandbox instead of letting the agent hit a 401 mid-task. A detached or CI run cannot answer the approval prompt, so approve interactively once or write the binding to ~/.config/sbx/credentials.yaml first.

3. Give the agent a task that needs the live web. Documentation sites are blocked under balanced, so this one has to go through Firecrawl.

It has been revealed that the kit’s instructions tell the agent to scrape blocked hosts through Firecrawl, so it calls fc.scrape(...) unprompted. Its response, trimmed:.

4. Verify each layer. In the same session, ! runs shell commands inside the sandbox.

Expected: FIRECRAWL_API_KEY=proxy-managed. A real fc-... value here means the key came from somewhere other than the kit.

Expected: the page as markdown, starting with # Changelog and the latest version heading. The same URL returns a 403 to curl from inside the sandbox, so output here proves the SDK, the credential, and the network rule at once.

The kit also describes itself inside the sandbox. This prints the published descriptor, and the agent instructions sit next to it as firecrawl-context.md:.

According to recent reports, running from source. To review or modify the kit before you run it, clone the repository and point --kit at the firecrawl/ directory; sbx builds source kits on demand:.

In a recent development, with the kit installed, the agent can look things up on the web while it works. The sandbox only needs to talk to one upcoming address, api.firecrawl.dev, and Firecrawl fetches the pages for it. This matters because the default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites. Without the kit, you’d have to allow each site one by one, and every new site you allow makes the sandbox a little less locked down.

Without the kit, you had a choice to make. The default balanced policy blocks most documentation sites, so you could either leave the agent working from what it remembered, or allow sites one by one and loosen the sandbox a little each time. The kit avoids that choice. Your Firecrawl API key stays on your machine, behind the proxy, and the agent still reads the web as it is today.

The result is fewer made-up APIs, fewer failed upgrades, and less time spent correcting an agent that was confidently out of date.

The kit is published under the firecrawl organization on Docker Hub as firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl, with source, changelog, and CI on GitHub under Apache-2.0. The SDK pin is verified against PyPI’s package hashes at install time, and every release passes Docker’s kit-tck conformance suite in CI. Review the descriptor and allowlist before running it, as with any kit.

Pull the kit from Docker Hub: hub.docker.com/r/firecrawl/sbx-kit-firecrawl. Challenges and feature requests go to the GitHub repository.

Breaking: Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine.
  • Industry observers note that how it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint.
  • In a recent development, from there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker.

Industry observers note that how it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.

In a recent development, from there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region.

The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS.

If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally.

Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path.

In a recent development, on macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image.

I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file.

In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials.

In a recent development, the emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000.

Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it.

With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them.

Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account.

To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual.

Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process.

Industry observers note that when it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off.

How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates.

Industry observers note that with each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better.

If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change.

Industry observers note that one group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an matter for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository.

How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships.

In a recent development, security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation.

Industry observers note that if you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BEUC urges Brussels to impose tougher penalties over alleged barriers to switching services and controlling personal data.

Significant Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which states the industry's compliance with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice.

BEUC mentioned: "Big Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products.".

It has been revealed that the European Commission designated the six companies as gatekeepers in 2023, imposing obligations on specified core platform services such as search engines, messaging services, and app stores. The DMA aims to make digital markets fairer and more open to competition.

The devil is in the details. In the years since, the EC has lined up Amazon and Microsoft's cloud businesses for gatekeeper status. In March 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings against Alphabet over Search and Google Play, while separately specifying measures Apple had to take to meet its interoperability obligations. In 2024, Microsoft's browser rivals argued that Edge should also be covered by the DMA's gatekeeper obligations, and so on.

According to recent reports, BEUC is a fan of the act – it published a report on its consumer benefits in 2025 – but is less impressed with industry's implementation. Its latest analysis draws together evidence of potential breaches submitted to the Commission between June 2025 and June 2026.

In the case of Microsoft, BEUC stated that the company used "behavioural techniques" and "non-neutral interfaces" to elicit consent from users for data sharing across services – emphasizing benefits, while not explaining why a user might want to decline. The Windows behemoth is also accused of making it tricky to change defaults and stop behavior such as apps opening links in Edge or using Bing as a search engine.

"Microsoft also regularly prompts owners who have selected an alternative browser or search engine to switch to Edge or Bing using increasingly subliminal techniques, such as prompts coming from the device manufacturer, which undermine effective compliance with the DMA," BEUC stated.

Recent findings suggest that then there's Google, which was fined €890 million in July for favoring its own services in Search and restricting developers' ability to direct Play Store people to alternative purchasing channels. As with Microsoft, BEUC expressed concerns about the non-neutral language Google used to obtain user consent, as well as how it allegedly made it difficult to change default settings or uninstall gatekeeper applications.

The alleged behavior of Apple, ByteDance, Amazon, and Meta was also highlighted, with examples including Apple's restrictions on alternative app distribution and Amazon using interface design techniques to nudge users into handing over their data.

Apple revealed fresh terms for developers earlier this year in response to its App Store dispute with the European Commission, but BEUC said it was "concerned that the new terms do not resolve fundamental non-compliance challenges.".

Recent findings suggest that google did not respond to requests for comment from The Register. A Microsoft spokesperson told us: "We are continuing to engage with the Commission and industry at large to ensure Microsoft's designated platforms comply fully with the DMA.".

It has been revealed that an Amazon spokesperson told The Register “Our consent experience is clear and gives customers informed choice about how their personal information is used across Amazon services. We see that in practice.

“A seller that uses Amazon Stores in the EU can offer the same products on any third-party online marketplace or its own direct to customer website at any price, without affecting their eligibility to be highlighted as the Featured Offer. This is set out clearly in our DMA Compliance Report.”.

BEUC director general Agustín Reyna mentioned: "The era of cosmetic compliance must end. It is high time the Commission holds gatekeepers to account and imposes dissuasive penalties in all cases where they bypass the DMA's rules.".

The report has been shared with the Commission. Whether BEUC's allegations lead to further findings of non-compliance or penalties is now a matter for the regulator. ®.

#69612. The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1857 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Docker ↗ Open Full Page

The Trust Layer: Securing Agentic AI with Docker AI Governance

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Docker

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt.
  • A model decision is not automatically an authorized action.
  • Industry observers note that the answer can’t rely only on the model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the security problem changes once an AI agent can do more than answer a prompt. It can execute code, access files, connect to services, and call external tools. That creates a upcoming security question for enterprises: how do you give an agent enough freedom to be useful without giving it more access than it actually needs?

A model decision is not automatically an authorized action. That distinction becomes vital the moment an agent can turn a model output into an action in a real system.

Industry observers note that the answer can’t rely only on the model. Agent behavior can vary, while security controls need to be clear and enforceable. That means putting controls around the environment where the agent runs, what it can access, which tools it can use, and what happens when a policy allows or blocks an action. For a CISO, this creates a trust gap. Approving the use of AI agents means being able to answer more than whether the model is capable: what access does the agent have, where are those boundaries enforced, and what evidence is available afterward? The goal is to let teams adopt agents without making model behavior itself the security boundary.

Docker AI Governance approaches this through three areas: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

In a recent development, together, they address three practical questions security teams need answered: Where can the agent operate? What can it do? And can we see what happened?

In this article, I use “trust layer” as shorthand for the infrastructure between what an agent wants to do and what the organization actually allows it to do.

There is a related trust question too: what software artifacts are these agentic workflows building and using? Docker Hardened Images address that software supply-chain side of the problem, alongside the runtime controls discussed below.

Figure 1: The three layers of Docker AI Governance: Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility.

In a recent development, an agent needs enough access to get real work done. A coding agent may need to install packages, build containers, edit project files, or connect to external services. The security challenge is deciding where those actions are allowed before the agent starts taking them.

It has been revealed that docker Sandboxes give each agent an isolated microVM environment a lightweight virtual machine with its own Docker Engine, filesystem, and network. Docker AI Governance adds policy around that environment so security teams can control network and filesystem access centrally.

According to recent reports, network policies can allow or block specific domains, IP ranges, and ports. Filesystem policies control which host paths can be mounted into a sandbox and whether that access is read-only or read-write. These controls are enforced at the network proxy and filesystem mount layers rather than depending on the agent to follow an instruction.

It has been revealed that for an organization, that means the same boundaries can follow developers across their sandboxes instead of being configured differently on every machine. Teams still get the access they need for their work, but an individual agent cannot simply expand those boundaries on its own.

A developer can check the effective boundary before starting the agent:.

The key part is that the result comes from the active policy, not from an instruction the agent is expected to follow.

This answers the first governance question: Where can the agent operate?

Once an agent has a controlled place to run, the next question is what it should be allowed to do through external tools.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) gives agents a common way to connect to external tools, services, and capabilities, but that also expands what an agent can act on. For enterprise use, making a tool available should not automatically mean every agent can use it.

Docker AI Governance puts policy around MCP activity handled through Docker’s MCP Gateway. Administrators can control which MCP servers may be registered and what agents can do through them, including tool calls, resources, prompts, and approval requirements. These organization policies are written in Cedar, a policy language used to express authorization rules. When MCP policy enforcement is active, governed requests are denied unless a matching policy permits them. For example, a policy can permit read-only tool calls for a specific registered MCP server:.

In a recent development, here, readOnly comes from the MCP tool’s annotations. Those annotations are supplied by the server and are advisory, so this example relies on metadata provided by that server.

It has been revealed that this makes tool access an explicit policy decision rather than something left to each agent or developer to configure independently. A team can be given access to the tools it needs, while other servers or actions remain unavailable. Policies can also require confirmation for specific tool calls when an action needs an additional checkpoint.

One boundary is worth making clear: MCP policies apply to activity handled by Docker’s MCP Gateway. If an agent connects directly to a remote MCP server from inside a sandbox, that connection falls under the sandbox’s network policy instead.

With the environment constrained and tool access governed, we can answer the second question: What can the agent do?

Setting a policy is only part of the job. Security teams also need to know when that policy was applied, what action triggered it, and whether the action was allowed or denied.

According to recent reports, docker AI Governance records sandbox policy decisions and sandbox session events as structured audit records. Each record captures details such as the principal, action, target, decision, and time. The records contain governance metadata rather than the contents of prompts or agent responses.

Audit records can be kept locally or delivered to the cloud. With cloud delivery enabled, teams can search the organization-wide record, export it for further analysis, or forward events into existing SIEM (security information and event management) workflows.

According to recent reports, denied actions are especially useful. A team can see not only that an action failed, but that a governance rule blocked it and why. Allowed decisions matter too: they provide a record of how policy was applied while the agent was working.

Current audit coverage includes Docker Sandboxes policy decisions and sandbox session events. The same schema can support additional Docker AI sources as they become available.

That closes the third part of the governance loop: Can we see what happened?

Sources indicate that AI Governance controls access around the agent at runtime. There is a separate question that matters to the workflows those agents participate in: what container images and software artifacts are they building, testing, or deploying?

Docker Hardened Images provide minimal, secure, and production-ready container images, Helm charts, and system packages maintained by Docker.

In practical terms, this gives teams evidence about what is inside an image and how that image was produced. Docker Hardened Images include signed SBOMs, VEX information, cryptographic signatures, and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance. Instead of simply trusting where an image came from, teams can inspect what is inside it and verify information about how it was built.

Sources indicate that for organizations with additional compliance requirements, Docker also provides FIPS-enabled and STIG-ready variants through relevant DHI offerings. These capabilities sit alongside the broader DHI security and supply-chain controls rather than making any single standard the foundation by itself.

AI Governance and Docker Hardened Images solve different parts of the trust problem. Governance controls the authority an agent has while it works; DHI helps establish trust in the container artifacts that the workflow depends on.

Figure 2: Docker Hardened Images combine minimal container images with signed supply-chain metadata and verifiable build provenance.

Consider a developer using a coding agent to investigate an matter, patch a service, and use an approved internal tool along the way.

In a recent development, the agent begins inside a Docker Sandbox. It can work with the project and run the commands needed for the task, but its access is still bounded by policy. If it tries to reach a network destination or mount a host path that the organization has not allowed, the applicable sandbox policy can block that access.

According to recent reports, now suppose the agent needs an MCP tool to look up information from another service. The request goes through Docker’s MCP Gateway, where organization policy determines whether that server and tool are permitted. A routine lookup might be allowed, while a more sensitive tool call could require confirmation or remain unavailable altogether.

For governance activity right now covered by AI Governance Audit Logs, Docker records the policy decision and relevant session metadata. Security teams can see who initiated the activity, what policy-controlled action was evaluated, and whether it was allowed or denied. Those records can then feed the organization’s existing monitoring and SIEM workflow.

Recent findings suggest that if that same agent builds or tests a containerized application, the software entering the workflow matters too. Docker Hardened Images provide a more verifiable software foundation for that workflow, while AI Governance controls what the agent is authorized to do at runtime.

The model is still making decisions about how to complete the task. What changes is the authority around those decisions. The agent can work autonomously inside the boundaries the organization has defined, while access outside those boundaries remains a policy decision.

That is the practical value of the three layers working together:.

Sandbox Policies define where the agent can operate.

MCP Tool Governance defines what tools it can use.

Audit + Visibility shows how governed activity was handled.

Recent findings suggest that taken together, the pattern is straightforward: define the boundary, check it before the agent starts working, enforce it while the agent is running, and use the resulting audit trail to understand what happened. If a boundary needs to change, the policy changes, not the expectation that the model will simply behave differently.

According to recent reports, the challenge with agentic AI is not simply that agents can make decisions. It is that those decisions can now lead directly to actions.

That makes the boundary around the agent just as important as the model itself. Docker AI Governance addresses that boundary through Sandbox Policies, MCP Tool Governance, and Audit + Visibility: controlling where agents can operate, what tools they can use, and how governed activity is recorded.

Docker Hardened Images address a related supply-chain concern by helping teams work with smaller, verifiable container artifacts.

Sources indicate that the goal is not to remove autonomy from agents. It is to make sure autonomy does not automatically come with unlimited authority.

As agents take on more real work, that distinction will matter more and more.

Docker rolls out a new brand built on trust. Learn why Docker is evolving for AI agents, what stays the same, and how to run agents securely with Docker.

Docker publishes fixed images for both Java4Shell and the NGINX HTTP/2 in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog.

Learn how Docker AI Governance secures agentic AI with sandbox policies, MCP tool governance, and audit visibility to support controlled AI agent workflows.

#69611. Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

📅 10 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1723 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1723 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui.
  • Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes.
  • Sources indicate that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

Sources indicate that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

Recent findings suggest that all the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

Industry observers note that this is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

In Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

Industry observers note that that same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

According to recent reports, there's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

Industry observers note that this is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

In a recent development, the drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

Recent findings suggest that this is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

Background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

There are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

Recent findings suggest that AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

Industry observers note that the image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

Recent findings suggest that so far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:.

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

This isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

In a recent development, every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

Recent findings suggest that the same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node demonstrates up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:.

Industry observers note that now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:.

In a recent development, bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

Recent findings suggest that if you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

Really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes.

According to recent reports, analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo.
  • It has been revealed that I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition.
  • According to recent reports, AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt.

It has been revealed that I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

According to recent reports, AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS.

Industry observers note that headlinesTest your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough reveals a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub.

It has been revealed that what I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production.

Industry observers note that AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply.

Last week’s introduces Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus aims in all Cognito Regions.

According to recent reports, claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use.

In a recent development, amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

Industry observers note that amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges.

Amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only upcoming ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE).

The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – Fresh Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s Fresh with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:.

Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data.

How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems.

Latest Update: Meet the New Docker: Built to Run on Trust

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Docker is officially launching its upcoming brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.

Let’s start with the significant picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

Recent findings suggest that but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents?

That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a fresh Docker.

A newly introduced Docker, but a familiar story.

Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a new way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one massive constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment.

Enter a firm you might have heard of: Docker.

According to recent reports, together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.”.

Recent findings suggest that today, of course, the challenge confronting us is new and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers.

In a recent development, let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it.

It has been revealed that the qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us.

On the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way.

In a recent development, agents have introduced a new problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.

Agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.

Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.

In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the latest Docker is all about trust.

According to recent reports, trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves.

According to recent reports, trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise.

According to recent reports, trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this big alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in.

Most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not.

Recent findings suggest that as our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a new day for Docker. Something that notes and highlights, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore.

Something, dare I say, whale sized.

I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby.

Sources indicate that if you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation company, Motto, we landed on a newly introduced Moby for the new Docker.

Watch Moby’s transformation here:.

In many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a fresh era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby.

In a recent development, we’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our newly introduced website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.

Recent findings suggest that wherever this fresh era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

Chief Marketing Officer, Docker.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘I gave up at least $6,000 and I’d do it again’.

Welcome to Friday and therefore to another edition of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed tech support column in which we share your tales of cleaning up messes made by clients and colleagues.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Dennis" who told us he once ran a tech support business in a major US city.

"I got a call from a very well-known lawyer's office," he told On Call. "Over the two decades I spent supporting his office, this attorney and I became close friends.".

The attorney was also a good client because Dennis found himself billing a three-figure sum every month for malware removal that resulted from the lawyer’s – ahem – personal browsing habits.

Dennis eventually tired of malware removal and told his client to expect a substantial bill for the iMac he was about to buy as a replacement for his PC.

"I told him this would pay for itself in 18 months," Dennis wrote, because he figured it wouldn't get malware all the time.

"He actually said, with genuine concern: 'If you do that, you will make less money'.".

Dennis replied that he aimed to give his clients the best advice, and that on this occasion his counsel was to pay Apple instead of himself!

Sources indicate that "It took him about five years to stumble across anything that could harm that iMac," Dennis wrote. "When he did, I had no idea what to do: I had never seen an infected Apple product.".

So he did what all tech support people do: reinstalled the OS and crossed his fingers.

Dennis was rewarded when the machine came back to life, with all data and settings intact.

"I had given up at least $6,000 in support revenue by solving his problem and I'd do it again," he wrote, before winding up his story by letting us know "I retired five years ago. It’s still on his desk!".

Have you done less tech support to deliver more value? If so, click here to send On Call an email and charge us with the responsibility of telling your story on a future Friday. ®.
