#69600. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1588 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • It has been revealed that as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

It has been revealed that as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project demonstrated they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

Industry observers note that A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

Industry observers note that the model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

It has been revealed that each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

In a recent development, BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

Recent findings suggest that that regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

According to recent reports, this depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

It has been revealed that real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

According to recent reports, naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

According to recent reports, the next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Recent findings suggest that each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Sources indicate that both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

According to recent reports, across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

According to recent reports, the overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

It has been revealed that the next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the fresh merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

In a recent development, A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

According to recent reports, every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

In a recent development, the benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we strategy to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

In a recent development, will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Optional update fixes misleading Android error for versions 25H2 and 26H2.
  • According to recent reports, A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded.
  • Sources indicate that the problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Optional update fixes misleading Android error for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

According to recent reports, A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

Sources indicate that the problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again.".

It has been revealed that except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored.".

Cross-device authentication lets consumers sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID.

Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected.

Recent findings suggest that an authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets.

Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, owners can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®.

  • It has been revealed that our launch post introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries.
  • Agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview, including monitoring for agents that run outside Google Cloud. To request access, see the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

It has been revealed that our launch post introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries. It covered agents on Google Cloud, such as Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Many teams also run agents on other clouds: on AWS Lambda next to an inventory database, as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry, or on-premises next to a system that can't move. Those agents carry the same behavioral risks, and until now Agent Anomaly Detection couldn't review them.

Agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime. If those traces and logs reach your Google Cloud project, it can detect anomalous behavior wherever the agent runs. In this post, we explain what Agent Anomaly Detection needs from an agent on other cloud, then show what it found for an agent on AWS Lambda and an agent on Microsoft Foundry.

Agent Anomaly Detection reads the logging and observability buckets that you choose when you enable it. Telemetry from anywhere works when:.

Agents built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Python, version 2.12.0 or later, can produce this telemetry with ADK's Google Cloud exporters and a few environment variables, which the next section demonstrates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we launched a change that has been a long time in the making: The updated website for freedesktop.org, as well as the refreshed wiki.freedesktop.org are live now!

You can read the announcement here, this blog post elaborates a bit on it and on the background of the changes, as well as future plans.

The freedesktop.org website has been a wiki for a long time, which definitely was the right call in its inception. A wiki is very much in spirit of Freedesktop’s mission statement to foster collaboration between desktop environments and to be a place to create de-facto standards.

However, over the years, working with the wiki became a bit of an matter: Not only did we face multiple spam-apocalypses (which in part motivated the switch to IkiWiki in 2013 and resulted in us heavily restricting write access to the wiki), but it also meant that official project information, finished specifications, half-finished proposals and pages nobody had touched in fifteen years were all sitting next to each other.

Since 2000 when Freedesktop.org was started, the project has grown so much and has had so many associated projects and specifications over the decades that it is now very difficult for upcoming people to get an overview what is current and what state the software projects and specifications hosted by Freedesktop.org are in.

Having only a wiki as a large and somewhat disorganized pile of information did not help with that issue, so I worked to split things up: We now have a website as well as a wiki, using different designs to distinguish the two, and serving different purposes.

According to recent reports, the website at www.freedesktop.org will be the place for “official”, or rather, more curated information. Now that the upcoming website is live, its content is still largely that of the old wiki. Over the next weeks, I will be working on cleaning up its contents and listings. For example, I will clearly split active projects from archived ones, add missing ones, and also work towards synchronizing the specifications hosted on the former wiki / website with the ones listed on specifications.fd.o.

So, basically I will do an inventory check of Freedesktop. That work has already started, but until now, I could not make any public changes to not disrupt workflows or make my own future work harder by having diverging information in two places (website & wiki).

I also wanted to make it easier for people to find information on how to get involved with Freedesktop and associated projects, so the newly introduced website now has a more discoverable section for that.

It has been revealed that the latest website is a static site hosted via GitLab Pages and using Pelican. You can view its sources if you like.

Of course, we also still want to keep the Wiki and all of its rich history around! It remains the easy-to-edit place for collaboration on upcoming projects and specifications.

Sources indicate that wiki edits must now happen through GitLab instead of the old IkiWiki web interface. While this sounds like an additional barrier to edit the wiki, it is significantly easier than requesting an account on annarchy to edit the old Wiki through the web interface. It also still allows us to keep the existing history as well as spam protection measures. In order to use the wiki with GitLab Pages and to keep the history easily accessible and readable, I rewrote the Git history of the wiki to make it pretend that all changes always happened in a content subdirectory. So, if commit signatures are missing and hashes are different: That is the only reason why. There have been no content changes or other metadata changes (and we still have a copy of the pristine wiki Git repository).

For the fd.o wiki, we are now also using Hari’s IkiWiki template that is already in use on the X.org website and which is much easier on the eyes.

Sources indicate that at the moment, I am mostly concerned with ensuring that the change has not broken any existing links and all systems keep working. After that, the wiki 🡘 website deduplication work will start and we can modernize both the content of the website and wiki.

If you find a broken link, an outdated page or anything else that looks wrong, please file an issue or, even better, open a merge request.For the wiki, you are very welcome to just fix or otherwise upgrade the page directly.

I did reach out to all wiki editors and projects impacted by this change in advance, but since there are so many people and projects involved, it is always possible to miss someone or something. If you found a bug, need edit permissions, or need help with anything, don’t hesitate to ping me: You can find me as ximion in OFTC’s #freedesktop IRC channel, in the very recently created #xdg-specs channel on the Freedesktop Matrix space, or you can email me.

I do want to echo the announcement news post here: None of Freedesktop.org would exist without the people who filled it with life over the years and who worked on cross-desktop collaborative projects. I have read through a lot of wiki history and old project pages over the recent months, and it feels amazing to know how much work and passion people have poured into the projects and collaborative efforts over the years – no matter if they were successes in the end, or remained experiments. I am very thankful for all current, past and future editors of the website and wiki, as well as all project maintainers and contributors.

I also want to thank the Sovereign Tech Agency once more for supporting me in their fellowship program as a maintainer, which enabled me to work on this task among other things.

Thanks to all contributors, in whichever way you contribute to our free desktop ecosystem!

Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Notice's existence can be acknowledged without harming national security, but its precise demands remain under wraps.
  • The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.
  • The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Notice's existence can be acknowledged without harming national security, but its precise demands remain under wraps.

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.

The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.

The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government.

The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters.

The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month.

A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers.

For Apple, a organization that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected.

While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand.

At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens.

In August 2025, Gabbard revealed that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to people in the US.

Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators.

Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless.

Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not.

While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public.

Sources indicate that "Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest.

"We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed.

"That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now.".

The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026.

The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a latest order focused on British owners.

The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty, Privacy International, and two individuals.

Industry observers note that A government spokesperson noted: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public.

"A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a firm's communications systems or data.

In a recent development, "Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so.

"Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies.".

Industry observers note that apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs.
  • Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that.
  • And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

It has been revealed that GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so owners can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

It has been revealed that no extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

Sources indicate that that is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

In a recent development, the model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

In a recent development, the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Recent findings suggest that transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for upcoming architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Recent findings suggest that our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

Recent findings suggest that A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

Sources indicate that the kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

It has been revealed that the first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

In a recent development, these changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

Industry observers note that the initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

Sources indicate that if you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an concern with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Consultancy argues a 'clean core' makes agents easier to deploy – but Kingfisher is taking a different route.
  • Global consultancy PwC claims IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Consultancy argues a 'clean core' makes agents easier to deploy – but Kingfisher is taking a different route.

Global consultancy PwC claims IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch.

Recent findings suggest that the Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier. Selling that prospect, rather than incremental improvements to existing processes, could help IT leaders justify a migration.

Oracle and SAP are both trying to persuade customers to move from established ERP systems to newer platforms. For SAP, that means S/4HANA, preferably in the cloud. For Oracle, it means Fusion Cloud Applications. Moving from ECC or E-Business Suite, respectively, can involve root-and-branch changes to technology and business processes, rather than a straightforward software upgrade.

Recent findings suggest that thousands of organizations still rely on these aging, often heavily customized systems. IT leaders struggle to justify a costly, time-consuming migration when the reward appears to be doing the same meat-and-veg business processes slightly better. For example, a survey of SAP users last year found that 95 percent noted building a positive case for migration required substantial effort or was genuinely challenging.

Speaking to The Register, Jennifer Colapietro, PwC digital core modernization platform leader, said: "You're seeing it a lot more as part of the rationale for the business case for why they should upgrade, answering the question: 'Why now? What should we prioritize?' Certainly, AI and getting the value of AI, a key business case justification for that.

Recent findings suggest that "Folks have budgets for ERP, but now [funding for transformation is] being split because they also have budgets for AI. But there's synergies across them. If you look at moving to a clean digital core ERP, that will help them to realize the AI value faster... be able to turn on AI and be able to start to automate a lot of the processes and implement the agents. That helps to build the business case.".

SAP recently introduced Joule 2.0 while Oracle has declared Fusion Claw. With both of these newly introduced technologies, the vendors are promising customers they can build AI agents to automate business processes and perform some work that was previously done by humans. Colapietro argued that moving to more modern platforms makes deploying AI agents easier and more effective than adding AI capabilities around legacy systems.

"It is more challenging to apply AI to the older systems. We focus on the importance of a clean digital core as the foundation for getting the value and effectiveness out of AI and scaling AI responsibly. I think that's given," she noted.

An ERP replacement isn't the only route to AI, however. European home improvement retailer Kingfisher – which owns the B&Q brand in the UK – eschewed SAP's overtures to upgrade its ECC system, despite encroaching deadlines. Mainstream maintenance for supported ECC 6.0 versions ends in December 2027, with optional extended maintenance through 2030 at a premium of two percentage points on the existing maintenance base.

Kingfisher opted instead for third-party support from Rimini Street, building an AI strategy around its existing ERP system using a combination of technology from Databricks and Google.

AI might help sell an ERP migration to the board. It doesn't make replacing the ERP system a prerequisite. ®.

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • According to recent reports, AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.
  • It has been revealed that as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

According to recent reports, AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

It has been revealed that as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

According to recent reports, this builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

In a recent development, performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

Sources indicate that when results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

Sources indicate that the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

Sources indicate that the coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Sources indicate that the UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Industry observers note that once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents.
  • Nov 20, 2026 6 min read.
  • AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free local implementation of more than 200 of its services dedicated to the public domain under CC0, and claims that "thousands of autonomous AI agents wrote every line of code" in it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents.

Nov 20, 2026 6 min read.

AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free local implementation of more than 200 of its services dedicated to the public domain under CC0, and claims that "thousands of autonomous AI agents wrote every line of code" in it. As InfoQ reported at launch, it ships as a single Rust binary generated from AWS's 438 public API models and listens on port 9297. The week since has brought the first independent fidelity numbers and a divided practitioner reaction.

Pointing an existing SDK, CLI, or coding agent at the emulator is a matter of environment variables, after which the launch post by Daniel Abib claims, "your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do":.

The same shell serves an agent. In the post, Kiro is asked to create and read back a DynamoDB table and issues the ordinary CLI calls against the local endpoint:.

Matt Wood, AWS's chief AI and technology officer, argues that the loop matters because of what an agent does while a check is slow: "A coding agent can build a lot of software around an incorrect assumption." He also names the failure mode an emulator introduces:.

In a recent development, an agent learns from the environment it experiences. If the emulator accepts behavior that AWS rejects, training can reinforce a mistake. An agent might also discover a shortcut that succeeds only because of an emulator defect.

The fidelity scores exist to expose that gap: each release publishes per service how many tests pass out of how many were verified against real AWS, with the failing tests public too, and Abib asks readers to "read a score as a snapshot of a product that's improving.".

Senior principal engineer Matthew Goldberg traces the project to a three-line prompt given to Kiro, "the simplest prompt that I could think of without any expectation that this would work":.

Kiro came back after 15 minutes with a passable first version of an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). I refined my prompt and had Kiro build me the rest of AWS over the weekend. And it did. It obviously had gaps, but it was compelling enough that my team started using it to test our software that Monday.

In a recent development, the production version is built by three agent teams: "One team manages a test suite; one team finds issues in the emulator; and one team fixes those issues." Each fix must pass a gate that compiles the change and runs agent reviews for coding standards, security, and fidelity regression. "Our team hasn't written or reviewed any of the code," Goldberg writes, and describes what the gate carries:.

Sources indicate that if any of those checks fail, the change is sent back to the agent for rework; if they all pass, it is merged to mainline. We've seen thousands of issues fixed every day as hundreds of agents concurrently work on the codebase. Without this merge gate, we wouldn't trust what our agents are building.

Swami Sivasubramanian, in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog, recalls rebuilding a replication engine with Kiro that had taken his team four months by hand:.

According to recent reports, I supervised the agent for four nights before I saw that it had no way to check its results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.

In his telling, the engineer's job becomes "to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct.".

It has been revealed that the first measurements from outside AWS come from Kento Ikeda, an AWS Community Builder, who ran version 1.0.322 in GitHub Actions the day after launch. DynamoDB, S3 and SQS passed roughly 60 to 70 percent of their fidelity tests at service level and 80 to 100 percent on the operations its code called, while CloudFormation sat near 20 percent. The emulator matched AWS's error wording, but a new DynamoDB table stayed in CREATING for three seconds and rejected writes until then. "Being generated from API models only means the shape of requests and responses matches AWS," he writes, and places the tool between mocks and a real sandbox as a third layer rather than a replacement for either.

The launch post draws its hardest line at security:.

It has been revealed that don't use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn't evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Unimplemented operations return HTTP 501, telemetry is on by default, throttling, outages and regional differences are not simulated, and the repository does not accept pull requests. On Hacker News, one reader quoted the line on the security page that the emulator "never denies a request signed with its own key" and asked why IAM was left out:.

I think because the agents were only building on the public API surface, it's hard to build this part. But they should've tried and let the agents read whatever policy engines AWS has. Or maybe it's a way to prevent someone from trivially running aws-emulator as AWSaaS?

According to recent reports, the thread's first question was whether this was "just an exercise or a real product they are going to ship and maintain," answered by a commenter identifying as AWS staff with "It's a real product that we plan to maintain." Another counted "29,684 commits in a repository less than a month old" and noted it "does not instill confidence." On r/aws, the most-upvoted comment turned Amazon's own line around, calling agents that fix code "without human review" a terrible idea for a tool used to test before production. The reply was that the API specifications already exist and the SDKs are generated from them, so a server derived from a fixed contract is where agents can iterate until the tests pass.

The timing matters to the people in those threads. LocalStack's free Hobby plan now requires an account and prohibits commercial use, with paid seats from $39 a month, and several commenters had already moved to Floci. One of them put the AWS release in that context:.

But in the wake of Localstack's changes, the landscape has been full of slopware and low trust anyway. I don't think this is worse, for now at least.

Recent findings suggest that AWS's version costs nothing and can be forked by either project. Sivasubramanian states AWS "will share more about this work at re:Invent" in December.

Breaking: Probabilistic data structures in Go, part 2

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Antonz

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle.
  • Previously, we reviewed the following data structures: Bloom filter (for checking if an item is in a set), Count-min sketch (for counting items), HyperLogLog (for counting unique items), T-digest (for finding quantiles), and Top-k (for finding the most frequent items).
  • In this post, we'll talk about other probabilistic structures and compare them to the ones we've already covered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle. Does the set contain a certain item? How many unique items are in the collection? What is the 99th percentile in a stream of numbers? How similar are two sets? Unlike deterministic structures, the answers might not be exact, but in return, you can save a lot of memory.

Previously, we reviewed the following data structures: Bloom filter (for checking if an item is in a set), Count-min sketch (for counting items), HyperLogLog (for counting unique items), T-digest (for finding quantiles), and Top-k (for finding the most frequent items).

In this post, we'll talk about other probabilistic structures and compare them to the ones we've already covered. We'll look at how they work and what kinds of guarantees they provide.

All examples use unsure — a package that implements these structures in Go.

Binary fuse filter • UltraLogLog • Log-linear histogram • MinHash.

Recent findings suggest that A binary fuse filter is a set that trades certainty for space, like a Bloom filter1. It can tell you that an item is definitely not in the set, or that it probably is (which might be a false positive). The filter doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

According to recent reports, unlike a Bloom filter, a binary fuse filter is static: you build it once from all the items, and you can't add more later. In exchange, it uses less memory than a Bloom filter with the same false positive rate. For example, a fuse filter for 1,000,000 items with a 0.39% false positive rate takes 1.13 MB (9 bits per item), while a Bloom filter takes 1.51 MB (12 bits per item).

This makes binary fuse filters a good fit for data that is written once and read many times, like the key set of an immutable file in a database (to skip files that don't have the key), or a list of known bad items, such as leaked passwords or malicious URLs.

The fingerprint type (T in Latest[T]) determines the false positive rate and the memory use:.

The constructor takes an iterator of items to add to the filter and the expected number of items (0 if unknown). The number is only used to preallocate memory, so a good estimate makes the build faster.

You can check if an item is in the filter, but you cannot add or delete an item, count the number of items, or iterate over them.

Sources indicate that the filter2 is an array of b-bit fingerprints (for example, b = 8 for uint8). Each item is hashed to a 64-bit value h, which gives the item's fingerprint f (b bits computed from h) and three positions in the array (cells). The array is filled so that for every item, the XOR of its cells equals f.

Recent findings suggest that to check an item, you compute h, look up its three cells, and compare their XOR with f. For an item in the set, they always match. For any other item, the XOR is a random b-bit value, which matches f with probability 2^-b.

Each check reads three cells, so for large filters it's three cache misses, against one for a blocked Bloom filter. However, since the reads are independent, the CPU can do them concurrently, so the checks are about as fast as with a Bloom filter.

Industry observers note that the filter uses the local wyhash3 implementation for hashing. It performs roughly the same as xxh34 but has a much simpler implementation, without SIMD or assembly.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks5, comparing unsure to xorfilter6 (binary fuse by the authors of the paper) and bloom (unsure's own Bloom filter) with 8-bit fingerprints (ns/op, lower is better):.

Memory, bits per item (lower is better):.

Recent findings suggest that unsure is the same size as xorfilter (same layout) with up to 25% faster checks. Compared to the Bloom filter, it uses up to 36% less memory, with checks as fast or faster, but up to 2.5× slower builds.

According to recent reports, ultraLogLog is a unique items counter that trades accuracy for space, like HyperLogLog7. It tells you approximately how many distinct items it has seen, no matter how many times each one appeared. UltraLogLog doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

Sources indicate that ultraLogLog is a newer design (Otmar Ertl, 2024) that uses the space more efficiently: for the same error, it needs about 43% less memory than HyperLogLog. For example, a HyperLogLog sketch with 0.81% standard error takes 16 KB, while an UltraLogLog sketch with 0.86% error takes 8 KB. However, adding, counting, and merging are slower than with HyperLogLog.

UltraLogLog is useful in the same places as HyperLogLog: counting unique visitors, unique search queries, or distinct values in a database column, possibly across many machines or segments.

You can merge sketches to get the total number of unique items from all of them, without counting shared items twice.

The sketch has one setting: the precision p, which gives a relative standard error of 0.782/√(2^p). The default is p=13 with 0.86% error in 8 KB, close to the common HyperLogLog default (0.81% in 16 KB).

You can add items to a sketch, get the estimated count, and merge sketches. You cannot check if a specific item was added, remove items, or list them.

In a recent development, hyperLogLog hashes each item and uses the first p bits of the hash to pick one of m = 2^p registers. It calculates the rank (the number of leading zeros in the rest of the hash, plus one) and keeps the highest rank it has seen in the register. Seeing a rank of k suggests there were about 2^k items in the register. The count is estimated from all the registers together.

A HyperLogLog register loses some information: it only keeps track of the highest value, not whether any slightly lower values were seen. These lower values show up at least as often as the highest one, so they can tell a lot about the count.

Sources indicate that ultraLogLog8 uses the registers more efficiently. Each register is still one byte, but it stores the highest rank k in the upper 6 bits, and whether k−1 and k−2 were seen in the lower 2 bits:.

The count estimate uses the FGRA estimator from the UltraLogLog paper. Each register adds a weight based on its value, and the count is calculated as a power of the sum of the weights. Nearly empty and nearly full sketches get special handling, so the estimate stays accurate from zero to billions of items, without bias tables or a separate formula for small counts.

It has been revealed that unsure keeps a histogram of register values (256 four-byte counters, 1 KB) updated as the registers change. This way, Count reads the histogram instead of scanning all the registers. Merge checks 8 registers at a time using a few bitwise operations to find which ones the other sketch would change, and only updates those.

The item is hashed once with wyhash, and the 64-bit hash is split into the register index and the rank.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks9, comparing UltraLogLog to unsure's own HyperLogLog and axiom10 (HyperLogLog with LogLog-Beta estimator and sparse mode) (ns/op, lower is better):.

Accuracy and memory, relative RMSE over 1,000 sketches (lower is better):.

In a recent development, ultraLogLog provides the same accuracy as HyperLogLog with almost half the memory. However, adding, counting, and merging are noticeably slower.

UltraLogLog paper by Otmar Ertl, 2024. ↩︎.

axiomhq/hyperloglog by Axiom. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that A log-linear histogram is a summary of a stream of numbers that trades accuracy for space. It can give you an approximate median, 99th percentile, or any other quantile of the data. It can also estimate what fraction of the numbers are below a certain value (the CDF). The histogram doesn't store the numbers, so it's much more compact than a sorted list.

According to recent reports, for example, to find the exact 99th percentile of 1,000,000 response times, you'd have to keep all of them. With 64-bit floats, that takes 8 MB. A log-linear histogram estimates the same percentile within 0.39% of its true value using about 14 KB — almost 600 times less.

The error is relative to the value: if the true 99th percentile is 200 ms, the histogram returns a value between 199.2 and 200.8 ms. This guarantee applies to every quantile, from the median to the most extreme outliers. The size of the histogram doesn't depend on the number of values, only on the accuracy you choose and on how wide the range of the values is.

A log-linear histogram is useful when you need percentiles for positive values that cover a wide range, like latencies, file sizes, or prices.

According to recent reports, you can merge histograms to gather data from multiple machines or segments (like by hour, endpoint, or region). Merging is exact: a merged histogram is the same as if it had received all the values directly.

The histogram has two settings: relative error and value range. By default, the error is 0.0039 (0.39%) and the range is from 1e-9 to 1e18. Lowering the error or increasing the range uses more memory.

You can add numbers to a histogram, estimate quantiles and the CDF, and merge histograms. You cannot remove numbers or list them.

A histogram splits the range of values into buckets and counts how many values are in each one. To estimate a quantile, it adds up the counts starting from the lowest bucket until it reaches the requested rank, then returns a value from that bucket. The accuracy of the estimate depends on how wide the bucket is.

With buckets that have equal widths, like 0–10, 10–20, and so on, every estimate has the same absolute error of ±5 around the bucket's midpoint. So the relative error is very large for small values and unnecessarily small for large values:.

A logarithmic histogram solves this by making each bucket's width proportional to its value. For example, if the bucket boundaries are powers of 1.02 (1, 1.02, 1.0404, ...), the end of each bucket is 2% larger than its start, so any value in the bucket is within about 1% of the bucket's midpoint. DDSketch11 uses this method. The downside is that finding the right bucket for a value means you have to calculate a logarithm, which is relatively slow.

Recent findings suggest that A log-linear histogram gets almost the same result with cheaper math. First, it splits the values into ranges between powers of two: 1–2, 2–4, 4–8, and so on (these are called octaves). Then it splits every octave into the same number of equal-width buckets. For example, here are three octaves with 4 buckets each:.

It has been revealed that each octave is twice as long as the previous one, so its buckets are twice as wide, and the bucket width grows with the values, as in a logarithmic histogram. Finding the right bucket only takes a few bit operations instead of calculating a logarithm.

Recent findings suggest that hdrHistogram12 is the best-known log-linear histogram. It records integers: the position of the highest 1 bit of a number determines its octave, and the next few bits determine the bucket within the octave.

Unsure works with float64 numbers and finds the bucket in a similar way to HdrHistogram.

IEEE 754 double-precision format.

A float64 in Go (and most other languages) is made up of three parts:.

The number's value is 1.f × 2^e, where 1.f is a binary fraction between 1 and 2.

In a recent development, the exponent determines the octave, from 2^e to 2^(e+1). The top m bits of the mantissa determine one of the 2^m equal buckets within the octave.

It has been revealed that for example, here's the number 5.25 with m=3 (8 buckets per octave). In binary, 5.25 = 1.0101₂ × 2², so the exponent is 2 (stored as 1025), and the mantissa starts with 0101:.

Add finds the bucket for the given number and increases the count. Merge adds the counts bucket by bucket. Quantile adds up the counts from the closer end (the leftmost bucket for q ≤ 0.5, the rightmost bucket otherwise) until it reaches the rank.

According to recent reports, the number of mantissa bits m comes from the requested error: the constructor picks the smallest m for which the maximum error doesn't exceed the requested one. The default is m=7: 128 buckets per octave and an error of 0.39%.

A t-digest13 also estimates quantiles, but it limits the error in ranks: Quantile(0.99) returns a value whose rank is close to 99%. A log-linear histogram limits the error in values: Quantile(0.99) returns a value close to the true 99th percentile.

In the middle of the data, the two are pretty similar. But in a long tail, values at nearby ranks can be very different, so even a small error in rank can lead to a major difference in value. Here is the mean relative error of an 8.5 KB t-digest (δ=100) on 1M values from three distributions: lognormal (as in the benchmarks), Pareto with α=1.5 (a longer tail), and uniform between 1,000,000 and 2,000,000 (no tail):.

A log-linear histogram of about the same size (1% error, 8 KB) has an error below 0.78% for all these cases.

Recent findings suggest that so a log-linear histogram is better for latencies, sizes, and other positive measurements with long tails. A t-digest is better when you need a fixed size no matter what the values are, or when the values can be arbitrarily close to zero.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks14, comparing unsure to hdr15 (log-linear, integers only, fixed range) and dd16 (DDSketch, logarithmic buckets) with a lognormal distribution (ns/op, lower is better):.

Mean relative error at the requested 0.1%, over 1M values (lower is better):.

Memory after adding 1M values (lower is better):.

Unsure adds values as fast as hdr and 5× faster than dd, queries 5–19× faster than hdr and about 35× faster than dd, and merges about as fast as dd and 35–175× faster than hdr. It's slightly less accurate than hdr (using 5× less memory), and more accurate than dd (using 1.4× more memory).

MinHash estimates how similar two sets are. It summarizes each set in a short fixed-size signature (for example, 256 numbers). Comparing two signatures gives the approximate Jaccard similarity of the sets: |A∩B| / |A∪B|, the proportion of unique items that both sets share.

The size of a signature doesn't depend on the size of the set, so you can compare two sets of a million items each just by comparing 256 pairs of numbers instead of checking every item. Plus, each set's signature is only calculated once, so comparing lots of sets to each other is relatively cheap.

MinHash is useful for finding near-duplicate documents, like web pages or essays (represented as sets of words or 3-word phrases). It's also useful for finding similar user profiles (as sets of liked items) or overlapping datasets (as sets of keys).

Industry observers note that the MinHash sketch has one setting: the signature size k, which gives a standard error of √(J(1−J)/k) for true similarity J. For example, with k=256 and J=0.5:.

You can add items to a sketch, merge sketches, and get and compare signatures. You cannot check if a specific item was added, count the items, remove them, or list them.

Classic MinHash17 hashes every item with k different hash functions. Here are two sets, A = {fox, cat, dog, owl} and B = {fox, dog, emu}, and their item hashes for k=4:.

In a recent development, for each hash function, the set keeps only the smallest hash value among its items. These k minimums are the set's signature. To estimate the similarity of two sets, compare their signatures position by position, count the number of equal values, and divide by k:.

The estimated similarity (0.5) is different from the actual value (2 shared items / 5 distinct items = 0.4). To get a more accurate estimate, k is usually much larger than in this example.

One permutation hashing18 hashes every item once, with a single hash function, and splits the range of hash values into k equal buckets. Each bucket keeps the smallest hash value among its items. Here are the same sets with k=4, using h1 from above:.

Recent findings suggest that each bucket works like a separate MinHash over the items in its range. So the bucket minimums form a signature, and comparing two signatures works the same way. But there is a catch: when a set isn't much larger than k, some buckets end up empty (shown as · above), so there's nothing to compare in them.

Optimal densification19 solves this by filling each empty bucket with the value from another bucket in the same set. Each empty bucket tries other buckets in a pseudo-random order and copies the value of the first non-empty one:.

Recent findings suggest that this order depends only on the empty bucket's position, so two similar sets tend to fill empty spots with the same values. This makes the estimate work for sets of any size, with about the same error as classic MinHash.

In a recent development, unsure keeps the k bucket minimums in the sketch. Add and Merge use the original buckets. Densification only happens in Signature, and it makes a copy of the buckets without modifying the sketch.

Recent findings suggest that each item is hashed once with 64-bit wyhash. Multiplying the hash by k once gives both the bucket and the value to store:.

Densification fills empty buckets in a coordinated way, spreading the copies evenly across the non-empty buckets. This keeps the error close to classic MinHash, and makes densification fast even for small sets.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks20, comparing unsure to dgryski21 (classic MinHash) (ns/op, lower is better):.

RMSE of the similarity estimate at k=256 and J=0.5 (lower is better):.

Unsure adds items 6–70× faster than dgryski, compares signatures at the same speed, has roughly the same accuracy, and uses half the memory.

Sources indicate that classic MinHash paper by Andrei Broder, 1997. ↩︎.

According to recent reports, one permutation hashing by Ping Li et al., 2012. ↩︎.

Industry observers note that optimal densification paper by Anshumali Shrivastava, 2017. ↩︎.

dgryski/go-minhash by Damian Gryski. ↩︎.

Bloom filter and HyperLogLog are everyone's favorites, but they're not the only useful probabilistic data structures out there. In some situations, you might find these helpful:.

To use them in Go, try the nalgeon/unsure package:.

Latest Update: Microsoft suggests Registry hack to work around hotpatch woes

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (337 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • App problems in Windows after default hotpatching?
  • Some Windows 11 applications might fail to install or launch after Microsoft's November hotpatch, but not to worry: there's a Registry tweak to work around it.
  • Microsoft has confirmed it isn't administrators' imaginations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

App problems in Windows after default hotpatching? Who could have foreseen that?

Some Windows 11 applications might fail to install or launch after Microsoft's November hotpatch, but not to worry: there's a Registry tweak to work around it.

Microsoft has confirmed it isn't administrators' imaginations. The November hotpatch is causing application errors, including in little-used and obscure apps such as Outlook.

Sources indicate that affected applications may fail during installation, launch, or use, displaying errors such as "ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED (0xC0000099)." Microsoft's investigation points to applications that load the 32-bit Windows Installer DLL, msi.dll. The problem is more common with 32-bit software, but can also affect 64-bit applications "under certain circumstances.".

Recent findings suggest that the workaround involves fiddling with the Registry on affected devices, so is not for the faint of heart and a backup is a good idea before diving in. Microsoft claims the key "HotPatchTableSize" in the folder "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management" needs to be set to "2000" followed by a restart.

Just the thing to round out the week for administrators.

The problem affects the November hotpatch, not the standard monthly cumulative security update. "Devices which installed the November 2026 Windows monthly security update are not expected to be affected by this issue," Microsoft remarked.

In a recent development, windows hotpatches are security updates that don't require a device restart (unless, as in this instance, administrators have to do so to address errors after a hotpatch is installed). Windows 11 hotpatching requires version 24H2 or later, an eligible subscription, and the necessary management and security configuration.

"Hotpatch upgrade package size is significantly smaller than the standard cumulative updates," Microsoft said, and the goal is to "streamline the installation process and enhance compliance efficiency.".

The offending hotpatch, KB5132043, was released on November 10. It followed the October 13 baseline, which was a prerequisite.

Microsoft made hotpatching the default in Windows Autopatch earlier this year. At the time, we asked: "What could possibly go wrong?".

Thanks to November's hotpatch, we have our answer. ®.
