Welcome RL Environments to the hub

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • Industry observers note that an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • Recent findings suggest that an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the latest RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

Industry observers note that an environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

Recent findings suggest that an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the latest RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

In a recent development, we think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

Industry observers note that the frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

In a recent development, harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer reveals the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Industry observers note that here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

Recent findings suggest that the command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:.

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:.

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

The docs have the full reference.

Industry observers note that we opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

Sources indicate that the bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier.
  • Building software takes more than a good prompt.
  • As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Blueprint, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

It has been revealed that see if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan.

What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped concerns, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

Recent findings suggest that you’re ready to turn that strategy into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

Industry observers note that writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

After spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

That review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

Sources indicate that smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard reveals intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

Figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up complications, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next plan starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

In a recent development, take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

Sources indicate that you don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count says you are.

We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”.

Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Windows Search gets a makeover, while Hello lights up dim rooms.
  • Microsoft has delivered its final scheduled non-security preview patch of 2026 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, with an updated Windows Search experience and a brighter Windows Hello for owners who prefer darker rooms.
  • Industry observers note that the optional KB5132057 enhancement arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Windows Search gets a makeover, while Hello lights up dim rooms.

Microsoft has delivered its final scheduled non-security preview patch of 2026 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, with an updated Windows Search experience and a brighter Windows Hello for owners who prefer darker rooms.

Industry observers note that the optional KB5132057 enhancement arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday. Microsoft is skipping December's non-security preview because of reduced holiday operations, though that doesn't cancel the monthly security release. This last preview is quite a doozy.

In a recent development, the big-ticket item is the "newly introduced Windows Search Experience." We saw a preview of this last month, and Microsoft has gone well beyond the "just make it work" request of many Windows consumers. Results appear faster with less clutter, the tool uses memory better, and files can be previewed directly in Windows Search.

Sources indicate that we're less convinced by inline actions, which let users perform common tasks directly through Windows Search without opening Settings. In our testing, "turn on dark mode" worked, but "switch on dark mode" did not, thus highlighting the limitations of the tool. In addition, we remain unconvinced that Windows Search is the place to run actions.

That stated, anything that makes Windows Search less of a punchline for unkind jokes about performance and accuracy is welcome, as are other features, including an optional screen-brightening feature for Windows Hello facial recognition in dim rooms, and the PowerToys-esque Run dialog, which consumers can enable in Settings.

While some of the new features won't be enabled immediately, Microsoft has included fixes that will be available right away. One addresses an matter where Windows Fax and Scan could fail to connect to a fax server. Handy for those occasions when email falls over into a heap.

There are also fixes for Windows IoT Enterprise LTSC activation failures and the misleading "Something went wrong" message shown on Android devices during cross-device passkey authentication. At the time of writing, Microsoft still lists the problem as something for which "we are working on a resolution to be released in a future Windows enhancement.".

Sadly, not everything has been pushed off the naughty step. SQL Server queries using OLE DB providers can still leave connections to external databases open after they've finished. Microsoft is working on that one and "will provide an update in an upcoming release." ®.

Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that holo4 is our latest series of agentic models.
  • Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that holo4 is our latest series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Recent findings suggest that holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

According to recent reports, OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Industry observers note that trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

It has been revealed that the tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Industry observers note that four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Holo4 27B (84 calls, 1.3M tokens).

Qwen3.8 27B (60 calls, 1.0M tokens).

Recent findings suggest that build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H organization logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Holo4 27B (94 calls, 1.5M tokens).

Qwen3.8 27B (118 calls, 1.9M tokens).

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines).

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines).

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Sources indicate that opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to fresh foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

In a recent development, these gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Sources indicate that both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

Article: Building Reliability Into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage Articles Building Reliability Into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover.
  • Nov 20, 2026 16 min read.
  • Recent findings suggest that I almost titled this section The Failure I Should Have Expected, and honestly, that would have been the more accurate title.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Articles Building Reliability Into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover.

Nov 20, 2026 16 min read.

Recent findings suggest that I almost titled this section The Failure I Should Have Expected, and honestly, that would have been the more accurate title. The conditions were all there. I just hadn't looked at them as a system that would eventually fail, only as infrastructure that had been working fine so far. My team owned a Terraform execution platform. The registry was backed by S3, which is standard stuff. Nothing else exotic was added. One morning the dashboard lit up, showing registry failures and artifacts not downloading. We declared an incident and started the usual process of elimination.

Two hours into our investigation, I was still convinced we had done something wrong. Perhaps we had a misconfigured bucket policy or added a permissions boundary incorrectly. Hopefully, this problem was  embarrassingly fixable. I kept going back to our changes, our config, and our code. The problem wasn't in any of those places.

Sources indicate that the actual cause took hours to surface. S3 signed URLs worked fine. You could manually call one and download an artifact without issue. But Terraform calls those URLs in sequence. When it resolves module dependencies, it fires a bunch of them back-to-back. Some of those requests were silently failing. Not all of them failed and not  in any consistent pattern, just... some, which was enough, to break the pipeline. From every dashboard we viewed, it looked like a registry bug, rather than an S3 bug.

In a recent development, find the bugs your tests miss. Antithesis uses deterministic simulation to explore thousands of failure scenarios, uncovering hard-to-reproduce bugs before they reach production. See how it works.

It has been revealed that we found the real cause by building a controlled test environment on my laptop. The failures were intermittent and appeared only in production, where experimenting is discouraged, so I needed a safe way to reproduce them. I wrote a small Terraform configuration that downloads modules from our registry, the same path our pipelines use, and ran it under a load test. I also checked out the Terraform source and added logging for HTTP request and response headers. Logging exposed an easy-to-miss detail. Terraform hands module downloads to HashiCorp's go-getter library, which sends a HEAD request to each signed URL before the GET, to check whether the download can be resumed. The load test reproduced the failure within ten minutes; the logs traced it to that HEAD request rather than to our registry. I proposed that a recent change in how AWS handled the HEAD request was producing the downstream 404.

Sources indicate that this hypothesis was initially not obvious even to their support personnel. I substantiated it with clear reproduction steps and diagnostic evidence. After they escalated internally to their architecture team, they confirmed that a recent change in request handling was the root cause and rolled back the change, restoring expected behavior. The lesson I took from this situation was when a managed dependency fails intermittently, reproduce your client's exact call pattern outside of production and instrument the client, not just the server.

Detection took a few hours. Recovery took nearly twenty-four hours, most of which was spent on support calls proving the issue was on their end waiting for AWS to acknowledge other customers were affected and waiting for the rollback to ship. Once AWS rolled back the S3 deployment, concurrent signed URL requests stabilized and the registry recovered without any changes on our end.

The mechanism here, signed URLs, concurrency, isn't the crucial part. The important part is the assumption I had been running on without examining it, that cloud infrastructure is reliable by default. That 99.99 percent is essentially "always works". I had treated the SLA like a guarantee rather than a statistical claim about a distribution with a tail I just hadn't seen yet.

Recent findings suggest that fifty-two minutes and thirty-six seconds of downtime per year. Considering the scale at which we were operating, hitting that window was not a matter of if, because I already had and more than once. I just hadn't treated it as evidence that my design needed to change.

It has been revealed that every organization I have worked for has made the same mistake and I bet that yours has too. Someone builds an observability system early on. They care about it. The dashboards are thoughtful, the alerts are calibrated, and the runbooks are linked. Then the system grows, engineers move on, haphazardly adding and wiring  in new services without anyone updating what came before. The people who built the original dashboards aren't around to upgrade them and the people who are around are nervous to touch something they didn't build and don't fully understand. Alerts drift out of calibration and dashboards start showing complications nobody on the current team knows how to interpret.

According to recent reports, then something breaks at a bad hour and the person on call opens Grafana and spends twenty minutes just trying to figure out what they are seeing. I have been in that position. The problem runs deeper than knowledge. It is a design failure, not a skills gap. The dashboards were built as a reporting layer, something that highlights you what is happening. But they were never connected to anything that does something about what is happening. The human is still the bridge between signal and response.

The mistake has nothing to do with tooling choice, query language, or dashboard layout. The mistake is treating observability as a way to inform humans rather than a way to drive system behavior. The difference is significant in practice. In reporting, a human receives an alert, interprets it under stress at a bad hour, decides what to do, and acts. In a control plane, the system receives and evaluates the signal against a defined policy, acts, and tells the human what happened. One of those scales with your headcount and on-call rotation, while the other breaks the moment both are stretched thin.

In a recent development, none of the tooling required for this design is upcoming. Prometheus has had alerting rules and webhook routing for years. Terraform can reconfigure routing weights. The components all exist; they just haven't been wired together with automation as the explicit goal. The pattern is the same at every scale, from pod autoscaling to regional failover: observe, decide, act, and confirm.

In a recent development, I have run Prometheus and Grafana stacks across hundreds of services, large builds and deployment pipelines, with thousands of executions per day. These tools are powerful but carry an operational cost teams consistently underestimate. Consider that expertise concentrates. When the person who really knows the stack leaves, calibration drifts silently until something breaks at the worst possible moment. Treat your observability stack with the same ownership model as your production services with regular reviews, real failure testing, and collective ownership that does not expire when the original author leaves.

Figure 1. Observability as a reporting layer vs. a control plane.The difference is whether a human or the system bridges signal to response. (Source: created by author.).

It has been revealed that I have never worked with anyone who needed a whitepaper to understand why multi-region matters. Instead, they needed an outage. After a major regional failure hit one of our cloud providers, the conversation about moving the Terraform registry to active-active architecture happened. The registry is called during every pipeline execution: every build, every deployment, and every release. When it goes down, every build, every deployment, and every release across every team stops with it. The blast radius of that dependency is much larger than it looks on an architecture diagram; it took a real outage for that to land viscerally for everyone involved.

We chose active-active, not active-passive. The reason for this choice comes up less often in architecture discussions than it should. We wanted the secondary region under real production load before we needed it for failover.

Active-passive looks good in diagrams. The failure mode is subtle and tends to surface at the worst possible time. The passive region has never handled your actual traffic. Its configuration has drifted unnoticed. Caches are cold and downstream dependencies haven't been exercised under anything close to real load. You have tested it in staging, maybe, with synthetic load that doesn't match your real traffic profile. When you fail under pressure, during an active incident with people watching, you discover all of these issues simultaneously.

I have been on that incident bridge. It is a specific kind of unpleasantry. You are trying to recover from one problem while discovering a second set of problems you didn't know you had. Active-active costs more. You have to keep regions in sync. Data consistency under partition requires careful thought. But when a region degrades, you shift load in a system that has been running in two regions all along, not making a leap of faith into an untested environment. We ran 50/50 under normal operation, which gave us continuous validation. Both regions were exercised constantly under real load. But 50/50 is the steady state, not the failure state. When a region actually degrades, traffic shifts to 100/0.

That transition is what you are building toward and it has to be tested deliberately. We ran chaos testing specifically for this situation. Cut one region entirely, verify the other absorbs full load cleanly, and confirm recovery when it comes back. If you haven't tested the 100/0 state, you haven't tested your disaster recovery (DR) system. Instead, you have tested your routing config. Multi-region is expensive to build and maintain. For a critical build-time dependency like this registry, it was the right call. But it should be a deliberate decision, not a default assumption.

Two failure modes in this design are worth being honest about, because neither reveals up in a clean chaos test. The first is a failure that is not regional at all. The S3 incident hit both regions at the same time, because both depended on the same S3 behavior. Regional failover cannot fix that problem. Failover shifts traffic to the other region, which is failing the same way, so failover triggers there too and traffic shifts back. The automation keeps moving traffic between two broken regions and adds noise to an incident it cannot resolve. Route 53 behaves the same way at the DNS layer. When every weighted record is unhealthy, it returns all of them rather than none. When both regions degrade together, the cause is a shared dependency. The correct automated response is to hold traffic where it is and page a human.

The second failure mode is a health check that reports the wrong thing. Our /health endpoint confirmed that the application process was running, not that it could do its job. If the backend database in one region goes down, the application keeps answering /health with 200 OK while real requests fail. This is exactly the case for which regional failover exists, but Route 53 sees a healthy endpoint and keeps sending traffic to the broken region. The confirmation Lambda checks the same endpoint, so it would also report a failover into that region as successful. A health check has to exercise the functionality the service delivers, such as a lightweight database read, not just confirm the process is up. Deep checks carry their own risk. If the dependency they test is shared by both regions, they bring back the first failure mode.

DNS TTL is the single most common DR misconfiguration I have seen in otherwise well-designed systems and it is worth addressing directly. TTL controls how long a resolver caches a DNS record before requerying. If the setting is too high (e.g.,  three hundred seconds, six hundred seconds, or whatever the module default happened to be) and your failover logic can fire correctly, then your routing weights can patch correctly and clients will keep hitting the degraded region for minutes because their resolvers haven't expired the old record. The failover executed correctly, but the traffic never moved because resolvers were still serving the cached record.

If the setting is too low, then you have built an overreactive system. A transient latency spike triggers a DNS change. The problem resolves thirty seconds later. Now you have regions flip-flopping and amplifying instability that would have cleared on their own. The right TTL is a deliberate number, chosen against your RTO, your health check interval, and your false positive tolerance. Most teams are running whatever default Infrastructure as code (IaC) module was set years ago. They don't know what that number is until they are debugging a failover that didn't go the way they expected.

Industry observers note that figure 2. DNS TTL and failover timing. A weight change that fires correctly can still leave traffic stranded in the degraded region until resolver caches expire. (Source: created by author.).

What separates DR systems that actually work from those existing only on paper is automation with confirmation, not just detecting failure, but acting on it and verifying the action succeeded. Most teams that have invested seriously in DR have detection, such as alerts that fire when error rates spike or health checks fail. Fewer have built the response layer, the automated action that runs when the signal fires. Fewer still have built the confirmation layer, the part checking whether or not the response actually worked.

Industry observers note that this last piece matters more than people realize. Automated failover without confirmation is a system taking an action and then going quiet. Did the secondary region receive the traffic? Did DNS propagate before the TTL window? Are the downstream dependencies there responding correctly? A system capable of answering these questions by continuing to observe after acting is one you can trust. A system that only fires and then goes silent is an untested hypothesis.

Industry observers note that the pattern looks like this in practice: A Prometheus alerting rule evaluates a composite signal, error rate above threshold AND p99 latency elevated AND sustained for a defined window. This observation is notable. Single-metric alerts are noisy. A transient spike fires them constantly for things that resolve on their own in a minute or two. The composite condition with a duration requirement indicates you only trigger degradation that has actually persisted.

Most implementations stop at the alert. Here the alert is the entry point to an automated chain. How traffic moves depends on the topology. In an active-active setup, Route 53 does the switching. Each regional record carries a weight and a health check. When a region's health check fails, Route 53 stops returning that record, so traffic shifts to the healthy region with no custom code. In an active-passive setup, the alert drives the switch. Alertmanager routes it to a webhook, which invokes a Lambda function that flips the Route 53 failover record to the secondary region. In both cases, the alert also triggers a confirmation Lambda that polls the target region's health endpoint until it confirms the region is returning healthy responses. The human receives a notification only after the Lambda confirms the loop completed successfully. Detection, action, and confirmation form one connected loop. Observability drives the action and then verifies the outcome.

It has been revealed that figure 3. The detect–act–confirm loop. Prometheus fires, Route 53 shifts traffic, Lambda polls until the target region confirms healthy, then notifies the team. (Source: created by author.).

That confirmation loop, in practice, looks like this:.

According to recent reports, the loop does not close until the health check returns 200. If it never does, the function returns unconfirmed and that signal itself becomes an alert, not a silent failure.

This is a Terraform configuration for the Route 53 side. Both regions carry equal weight and Route 53 stops returning a region's record when its health check fails:.

It has been revealed that the by (region) clause is what makes this rule region-aware. It evaluates the composite signal independently per region, so when one region degrades while the other remains healthy, the alert fires with the specific region label that tells the automation exactly which region is degraded.

Recent findings suggest that the for: 90s is doing real work there. Without it, this alert fires on blips. With it, the alert fires only when something has been consistently degraded for a minute and a half, which is a meaningfully different situation.

Finally, there is testing. The most effective practice I know for thorough testing is the game day,  a scheduled exercise where the team deliberately injects real failures into production systems and works through detection, response, and recovery in real time, with the people who would handle a real incident in the room. It is not a runbook walk-through in staging.

Game days find the human gaps as reliably as they find technical ones. Who actually has decision authority when you cannot reach the incident commander? Where is the runbook for this failure mode, exactly? Does everyone know? The first time most teams run one, the answer to these questions is uncomfortable. That is the point. Finding it during a game day costs an afternoon.

The validation that teams most consistently skip is testing that the confirmation layer correctly recognizes a successful failover and stops taking action. People test that the failover fires. They rarely test what happens if it fires and the system thinks it didn't work. That is a real path to cascading failures you created yourself.

The S3 incident wasn't something I had modeled. Nobody had a runbook for "S3 silently breaks concurrent signed URL requests under load following an internal deployment". The assumption that underpins a lot of how we build systems, that the infrastructure below us is basically reliable, is fine most of the time, which is exactly why it is so rarely questioned.

Industry observers note that three steps will turn your failover proposal into a working system. First, pick one alert that pages a human today and wire it to an automated response with a confirmation step. Second, put your secondary region under real production traffic before you need it for failover. Third, on your next game day, test the confirmation layer, not just the trigger. Verify that the system recognizes a successful failover and stops acting. If you haven't validated all three, you have a plan, not a system.

Infrastructure will fail, and the next failure will probably be one you haven't seen before. Whether a person has to piece together a response manually or the system handles it was decided long before the incident started.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Trade body warns automotive, medical, and defense orders are being crowded out, with relief unlikely before mid-2028.
  • The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies.
  • The Global Electronics Association says demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trade body warns automotive, medical, and defense orders are being crowded out, with relief unlikely before mid-2028.

The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies.

The Global Electronics Association says demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards.

Recent findings suggest that its report, "The PCB Squeeze: A Wake-Up Call for Global Electronics," states AI servers need increasingly complex boards. While a typical PC board has about 12 layers of tracks, AI server boards can have 40 to 60 layers or more, and each additional layer requires more resin, copper foil, and laminate.

The supply of materials is set to be constrained through at least the first half of 2027, the report says, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028.

Programs to deliver PCBs for automotive, industrial, medical and even the defense industries are being crowded out as AI soaks up scarce capacity, it claims.

The association's North American figures show orders growing much faster than deliveries. PCB bookings rose 56.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while PCB shipments increased 13.3 percent.

In a recent development, fabrication capacity is expanding, aimed at meeting the increased demand from the AI infrastructure sector, especially in Asia, where more than 90 percent of the world's boards are made. The report says that $10 billion has gone toward upcoming PCB plants in Southeast Asia, and at least as much has been invested in China over the past three years, but the raw materials are themselves constrained.

In a recent development, it warns of lengthening lead times for those raw materials. Standard FR-4 laminate now takes six to eight weeks to ship, up from two to three weeks a year ago, while advanced low-loss laminates now take 14 to 18 weeks for delivery, for example.

Tightening supplies usually lead to price increases, and the report claims that suppliers raised laminate costs by 30 percent in September, and that the price tag of some types of E-glass cloth for circuit boards has risen by 300 percent.

The report also puts copper prices up 37 percent over the past year. Concerns have been raised about copper supplies before, as The Register has reported multiple times.

The association compares the risk with the 2021 chip shortage, when disrupted supplies left manufacturers unable to secure even relatively mundane components.

New capacity is coming, but it is late and comes in dribs and drabs, according to the report, while AI demand just keeps on absorbing it as soon as it arrives.

The association's advice is for buyers to plan early, and to share realistic forecasts with suppliers rather than double-booking. Board makers should qualify alternative suppliers of materials such as laminate and copper foil before shortages bite, but it warns against stockpiling beyond real need, which adds to forward-buying pressure.

But it would like governments to step in, of course, by tracking board and material lead times with industry and offering tax incentives for investment in advanced PCB and substrate manufacturing equipment.

The wish list also includes state investment in research and development plus qualification of newly introduced alternative materials. It would like to see loan guarantees and grants to protect critical programs and small fabricators, structured so as to sustain new capacity if forward buying unravels and demand corrects in 2027.

"Yes, we are seeing constraint in upstream materials and have been reporting it for the past couple of quarters," stated Cori Masters, senior research analyst director for Supply Chain Operations at Gartner.

Sources indicate that "In addition, AI datacenter infrastructure build out is moving capacity support to high-layer count PCBs which increase throughput time and decreases availability of line utilization for more traditional PCB products," she told The Register. ®.

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1852 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • It has been revealed that consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

It has been revealed that consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

Sources indicate that A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

Sources indicate that this is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

According to recent reports, provenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

According to recent reports, the verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

Recent findings suggest that A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

According to recent reports, those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a fresh setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

In a recent development, we tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

According to recent reports, the most direct result is this: experts stated 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Recent findings suggest that binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

Industry observers note that in a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

It has been revealed that we also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This reveals it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

According to recent reports, blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

Sources indicate that that adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Industry observers note that want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

It has been revealed that source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

According to recent reports, practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

It has been revealed that hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Industry observers note that hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

GitHub availability report: October 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
  • Recent findings suggest that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
  • As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

Recent findings suggest that the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

Industry observers note that that capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

In a recent development, we also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

It has been revealed that reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in consumers. More details on these and other incidents follow.

In a recent development, the East US 3 buildout is about one week behind blueprint. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Industry observers note that customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Sources indicate that jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Recent findings suggest that duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

According to recent reports, customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Recent findings suggest that web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

According to recent reports, during regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

According to recent reports, customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

According to recent reports, an internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

In a recent development, some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

Industry observers note that we took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Industry observers note that customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

Recent findings suggest that copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

Sources indicate that customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Complications, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

Recent findings suggest that A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

Recent findings suggest that the pool was already running near capacity when some revision requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Sources indicate that follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.
