MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • Recent findings suggest that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and newly introduced Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

Recent findings suggest that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Sources indicate that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the significant matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Recent findings suggest that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

Recent findings suggest that in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Industry observers note that the decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Sources indicate that working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

According to recent reports, SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

According to recent reports, audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

Industry observers note that one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

Sources indicate that you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

According to recent reports, several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

Industry observers note that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

Sources indicate that the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

It has been revealed that bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Recent findings suggest that pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A major thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#69525. As cars go digital, US consumers pay an extra $12 billion a year for repairs

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (557 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

As cars go digital, US consumers pay an extra $12 billion a year for repairs

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today's vehicles need software tools to make repairs, and the subscriptions inflate insurance fees.
  • The computerization of cars comes at a price to US consumers, according to the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), which says that software fees and other charges faced by mechanics push up garage costs.
  • An investigation by the non-profit consumer group estimates that car repair costs for Americans have been inflated by $12 billion each year, as vehicles integrate more computerized functions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today's vehicles need software tools to make repairs, and the subscriptions inflate insurance fees.

The computerization of cars comes at a price to US consumers, according to the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), which says that software fees and other charges faced by mechanics push up garage costs.

An investigation by the non-profit consumer group estimates that car repair costs for Americans have been inflated by $12 billion each year, as vehicles integrate more computerized functions. Its report, Closing Shop, is available online.

To find a failed sensor, release an electronic parking brake, or perform diagnostics, a technician has to first connect a laptop or tablet to the vehicle. To so this, the repair shop has to have the right software tools, and that means paying the vehicle manufacturer subscription charges and other fees, in order to get the information they need to complete the job.

If smaller independent repair shops can’t afford all the necessary software or subscriptions, they may be forced to steer customers to authorized dealerships for some fixes – about one in five jobs – and this allows the latter to charge more.

Sources indicate that PIRG claims that drivers pay for this through their insurance premiums, even if they never need to get their car fixed, because higher repair costs mean higher insurance claims. It indicates the price of auto insurance has risen three times as fast as the rest of the US economy since 2012.

It has been revealed that even if mechanics do choose to pay for the software, they spend an estimated collective 83 million hours a year buying, downloading, logging in, and waiting. At typical repair rates, that adds up to $12 billion.

A separate report from the PIRG Education Fund claims that a two-tiered repair model now exists, where independent sites conduct repairs with less information, less powerful diagnostic tools, and higher associated costs than the authorized dealerships.

The advocacy group wants to see legislators take this matter in hand, and has a number of recommendations for them. One is to stop manufacturers from locking out independent mechanics from simple repair jobs like changing brake pads, and require them to support a standard protocol for authenticating independent diagnostic tools.

Another is to give owners control over their vehicle’s data via a standardized platform for accessing telematics repair information, so that the owner can give access to an independent repair shop. Car firms can use the vehicle data to tell owners that a repair is needed and to take it to an approved repair shop, without even disclosing what the issue is.

It has been revealed that DIY repairers should be able to get everything they need to fix their own cars. Service information and basic diagnostic software should be free, and PIRG also wants a cap on the license fees manufacturers charge for their official software tools.

“We’ve allowed car manufacturers to build a toll road between the mechanic and the repair,” notes Nathan Proctor, leader of PIRG’s Right to Repair campaign and co-author on the report.

“We have a plethora of tolls on the road – subscriptions you need for manuals, diagnostic tools, secure access and more. Not only are all these tolls expensive, they also create traffic jams, slowing down the whole process, which adds to the costs for consumers.”  ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

According to recent reports, local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

According to recent reports, the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too massive to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

In a recent development, reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the latest provider can't replay them.

It has been revealed that API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Sources indicate that community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Sources indicate that language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

  • Nov 21, 2026 3 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News How Google Traced GKE API Timeouts to a Linux Kernel TCP Bug.

Nov 21, 2026 3 min read.

Google recently detailed how three interacting bugs across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, and the Linux kernel caused intermittent Kubernetes API connectivity failures, blocking around 800 developers from deploying to production.

In January, a customer running multiple GKE clusters with Private Service Connect (PSC) for private control-plane access experienced intermittent timeouts when pods attempted to reach the Kubernetes API server.

Packet captures revealed that the control plane was responding to upcoming TCP connection requests with stale ACK packets belonging to previously closed connections. The root cause involved three separate bugs across different networking layers. Akash Thakur, senior technical solutions engineer at Google Cloud, describes how engineers across multiple Google teams identified three root causes and ultimately addressed them:.

Industry observers note that in a race to fix the problem, we involved engineers across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, networking, hostnet, kernel, and the Linux upstream community, who together tracked down not one but three distinct root causes. And the final fix landed not as a config change or a feature flag, but as a patch to the Linux kernel itself.

The investigation identified three interacting causes: packet reordering in PSC, Envoy's half-close behavior preventing TCP connections from being properly closed, and a Linux kernel bug that discarded certain reordered FIN packets.

Industry observers note that thakur describes a complex troubleshooting case involving I/O timeouts across Private Service Connect, virtual network interfaces, and the Linux TCP state machine, which ultimately revealed a kernel problem leaving sockets stuck indefinitely in the FIN_WAIT_2 state. Thakur explains:.

Most networking cases resolve at one layer. You find the misconfigured firewall rule, the exhausted connection pool, the miscalculated MTU. You fix it and move on. This one was different because the symptom — i/o timeout on a connection that never completed — was the same whether you were looking at the Private Service Connect layer, the kernel's TCP state machine, or Envoy's connection management. Every layer had a plausible explanation, and every explanation was incomplete.

The glitch was addressed through three coordinated fixes over several weeks: Google first rolled back a Private Service Connect change to restore connectivity, then corrected the proxy protocol handling and added regression tests. Finally, a Linux kernel patch, authored by Eric Dumazet, formerly a software engineer at Google, fixed the underlying TCP issue. Rohan Karne, managing director at Google Cloud, comments:.

This is the unglamorous reality of mission-critical platform engineering—methodically ruling out the obvious suspects and digging into packet captures until you find the kernel root cause.

Thakur highlights how individually reasonable behaviors across networking, proxies and operating systems can combine into complex infrastructure failures. Packet captures at multiple network layers were essential to identifying the problem, while correlating network symptoms with infrastructure changes helped establish the connection between the three bugs. Guangba Yu, a postdoctoral researcher at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, highlights:.

Recent findings suggest that for AIOps and chaos engineering, the transferable method is organizing simultaneous path observations, protocol state, and rollout events while distinguishing symptom recovery from state-machine correction. This anonymized case supplies no population failure rate and does not explain all API timeouts.

Justin Garrison, field CTO at Sidero, notes:.

At first I was excited to read this article that leads to a kernel patch which are always fun. It turns out GKE just runs a kernel from 3 years ago (6.1) and the bug was already fixed upstream and they had to backport it.

The kernel fix was merged into Linux 6.9.7 and backported to the 6.6 and 6.1 LTS branches, reaching GKE customers in version 1.33.5 and later.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love using JJ and recently I’ve found a cool way to handle TODOs that works for me.

Usually I’ll put them in a TODO.md file which is pretty standard. But, I forget about this file swiftly and am not very good at remembering to cross stuff off. Also since it’s in-tree I’ll often not want to patch it, and then forget to do so later.

Industry observers note that JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work. So what if I just make all the stuff I wanna do later as empty commits?

Pretty nice! When I want to start working on something I’ll rebase it out of my TODO tree and onto some other change.

I need to rebase my “TODO base” forward when i make changes, but because it’s empty it will never have conflicts and can pretty easily move around.

TODOs that depend on other TODOs also naturally fit here, I just make fresh empty commits on top of other empty commits.

I have git.private-commits configured to make sure nothing with the private: prefix will get pushed. This ensures my TODOs stay on my local system. Of course, there are benefits to not doing this.

Anyway that’s about it, not very ground breaking but something I like.

Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch owners had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

It has been revealed that torchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

In a recent development, the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

In a recent development, the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Recent findings suggest that TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

It has been revealed that models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

It has been revealed that the Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

It has been revealed that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

Sources indicate that we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

Sources indicate that the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an matter on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 concerns, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel looks. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch people. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an matter and tell us about it.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits unveiled since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.

It has been revealed that the motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.

It has been revealed that adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.

The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?

Industry observers note that for these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.

My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the vital quality criteria.

I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance challenges (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front.

Industry observers note that while desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.

It has been revealed that thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" blueprint for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop.

That mentioned, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view. You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit.

In a recent development, one of the big unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley. It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of new Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative.

AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design.

One topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This issue is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates.

According to recent reports, there has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU.

This is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not.

It has been revealed that one of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases.

Sources indicate that that’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and update the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor.

For this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting.

One theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering well is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well.

This philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished.

Industry observers note that I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of design and execution. Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine.

Having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically important. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular.

Recent findings suggest that that remarked, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors.

The Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality.

According to recent reports, blitz, as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical.

Recent findings suggest that one good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry, on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it.

Industry observers note that by contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing.

Given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring.

It has been revealed that one useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation.

Industry observers note that another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating new layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter).

According to recent reports, for a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI. Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance.

Thanks to Nico Burns for reviewing an earlier draft of this post.

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

It has been revealed that the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

According to recent reports, the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

Sources indicate that after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

It has been revealed that start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

In a recent development, after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

Sources indicate that the table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

According to recent reports, each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

Recent findings suggest that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

Industry observers note that in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

Industry observers note that the table highlights one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

According to recent reports, key_averages() indicates which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold.
  • It has been revealed that the BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold.

Sources indicate that the BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

#69512. Industry News: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2226 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • It has been revealed that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

It has been revealed that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

Industry observers note that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

In a recent development, the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

It has been revealed that the second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

In a recent development, the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

According to recent reports, think of a shipping organization that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

It has been revealed that and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

According to recent reports, adapting a model's vocabulary is not a upcoming idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

Industry observers note that they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

Industry observers note that first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Recent findings suggest that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping manufacturer: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

Industry observers note that to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

In a recent development, third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

Industry observers note that an expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents indicates up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

Industry observers note that A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

Industry observers note that to measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

According to recent reports, the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Recent findings suggest that getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

It has been revealed that the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Sources indicate that specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

QCon San Francisco 2026: Scaling Tech by Aligning Humans

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Scaling Tech by Aligning Humans.
  • Nov 21, 2026 3 min read.
  • At QCon San Francisco 2026, Scott Behrens, Principal Security Engineer at Netflix, presented how staff-plus engineers can define and align a company-wide technical strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Scaling Tech by Aligning Humans.

Nov 21, 2026 3 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Scott Behrens, Principal Security Engineer at Netflix, presented how staff-plus engineers can define and align a company-wide technical strategy. Drawing on Netflix's experience scaling internal AI agents, the talk argued that a strategy that brings people together can often scale impact further than any code an engineer could write alone.

Behrens explained that the work started when several product strategies, each with its own direction, began to share similar technical risks. Without a common technical strategy underneath them, teams were optimizing locally for different goals. His view was that technical strategy can complement product strategy without waiting for it, that lightweight strategies deliver faster than long technical documents, and that a clear north star does more steering than people expect.

Industry observers note that the talk presented a playbook organized as levels in a video game. The first step is finding the right problem. Behrens suggested looking at manufacturer communications, incident trends, technical debt, conversations with other tech leads, and gaps between team charters, then deciding whether the problem is worth solving now, whether it is foundational or compounding, and whether one is the right person to lead it.

Sources indicate that next comes the pitch. Behrens recommended a short problem statement that explains the intent, the expected value, the problems with supporting evidence, why the work matters now, and dated next steps. He suggested leaving possible approaches open so the people who join can shape them, and testing the statement early with a few colleagues, including the likeliest dissenter.

The presentation then covered building a small tiger team focused on creating the strategy rather than executing it. Behrens highlighted the importance of mixing perspectives, choosing people comfortable with ambiguity, getting manager support, and agreeing on scope, timeline, and a clear stop condition from the start. He shared that his first meeting had far too many people and still missed key functions, and emphasized that the most important trait of a good team is making it safe to push back.

With a team in place, the next step is a north star, a short aspirational statement that gives direction and helps answer whether a piece of work moves the organization closer or farther from its goal. Behrens noted that writing a good north star is harder than it looks, and recommended drafting it with the team and pairing it with key outcomes that define what must be true.

According to recent reports, the strategy itself, according to Behrens, is simply a set of choices. He described writing strategy bets as a choice versus another reasonable choice, naming the tradeoff explicitly, keeping each bet short, and revisiting them over time. If a bet does not feel a little uncomfortable, he mentioned, it is probably not a real bet. Keeping only a small set of active bets helps the strategy stay focused.

In a recent development, the talk also emphasized communication and feedback. Behrens suggested expanding support gradually from the immediate team to managers, directors, and executives, recruiting champions across the organization, and openly showing how feedback changed the strategy. Success, he said, is when you are not in the room and people can still explain the work. He also reviewed common failure modes, such as unclear problem statements, the wrong team, vague north stars, bets that are not really bets, and strategies that nobody knows exist.

The presentation concluded by encouraging engineers to keep strategy simple, communicate it widely, use a short north star to steer decisions, and adapt the playbook to their own context. As organizations launch more initiatives in parallel, especially around AI, the ability of senior engineers to align many teams around a shared technical direction may become as valuable as the systems they build.

#69509. What If Netscape Did SSL the HTTP Way?

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3540 w)
