What If Netscape Did SSL the HTTP Way?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Billpg

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when you visit a secure website today, your browser connects to port 443 and immediately starts speaking TLS.
  • Sources indicate that this is why so many good ideas from HTTP had to be reinvented, years later, inside TLS.
  • Let’s take a trip into a parallel universe where Netscape didn’t take the easy way out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when you visit a secure website today, your browser connects to port 443 and immediately starts speaking TLS. Only once the encryption is up and running does it get around to speaking HTTP. That’s two protocols stacked on top of each other, and the one at the bottom doesn’t know or care about anything the one on top has learned over the decades.

Sources indicate that this is why so many good ideas from HTTP had to be reinvented, years later, inside TLS. The most notorious is SNI, which is a Host header with extra steps.

It didn’t have to be this way. Let’s take a trip into a parallel universe where Netscape didn’t take the easy way out.

When Netscape released SSL in 1995, it came with a latest URL scheme (https://) and a new port number (443). Plenty of people grumbled. The web already had a protocol and a port, so why invent new ones? Why not secure the conversation you’re already having?

According to recent reports, to be fair to Netscape, in 1995 there wasn’t really a “proper” way to do that. HTTP/1.0 had no mechanism for handing a connection over to another protocol. The Upgrade header didn’t arrive until HTTP/1.1 in 1997, and the Host header, which made it possible to run many websites on one IP address, came with it. Netscape couldn’t have used either of them because neither existed yet.

But this is my parallel universe, so let’s say HTTP grew those headers a couple of years early and Netscape decided to wait for them.

Recent findings suggest that in our universe, a TLS connection begins with a ClientHello and the server replies with its certificate. In the parallel universe, that first exchange is just plain HTTP in the clear.

In a recent development, the browser wants to buy something from shop.example.com. It connects to port 80, the same as always, and asks for the server’s certificate.

Recent findings suggest that (Yes, /.well-known/ is from 2010. It’s a parallel universe. Let me have this one.).

The server responds with its certificate, and the certificates of any intermediate CAs, as an ordinary HTTP response. The browser checks the chain against its list of root CAs, exactly as it would in our universe. Is it signed by someone we trust? Is it for shop.example.com? Has it expired?

In a recent development, if you’re worried about sending the certificate in the clear, don’t be. Every version of SSL and TLS up to 1.2 sent the certificate unencrypted too. A certificate is public by design. An attacker can swap it for a different one, but they can’t make one that’s valid for shop.example.com without a CA’s help, and if they can get one of those, you have bigger problems.

In a recent development, once the browser is happy, it knows the server’s public key. It invents a random secret, encrypts it with that key and asks to upgrade.

Industry observers note that only the real server, holding the private key, can decrypt that secret. It replies with a random value of its own and switches protocols.

In a recent development, both sides now derive their encryption keys from the browser’s secret, the server’s random value and a hash of everything that was said in the clear up to this point. Mixing in that hash means that if anyone tampered with the plaintext part, the two sides end up with different keys and the connection fails. From this point on everything on the connection is encrypted, starting with the response to GET /checkout.

Industry observers note that I’m describing the 1995 approach, where the browser encrypted a secret with the server’s RSA key. When Diffie-Hellman key exchange came along, it would have been just a different pair of headers: the browser sends its half of the exchange, and the server replies with its half, signed by the key in its certificate. Changing how keys are exchanged becomes header negotiation, which HTTP is already very good at.

Browser: Hello, shop.example.com. Who are you?Server: Here’s my certificate.Browser: That checks out. Here’s a secret only you can read. Shall we go somewhere private?Server: 101.Eavesdropper: Aw.

The first thing we get for free is the one that took our universe the longest to sort out.

According to recent reports, that very first request for the certificate has a Host header. A server hosting a thousand websites on one IP address knows exactly which certificate to send back, because the browser told it, using a header the server already understands. There’s nothing to retrofit.

Sources indicate that in our universe, the server had to pick a certificate before it knew which website you wanted. For years, every secure website needed its own IP address, which was one of the reasons HTTPS stayed expensive and rare for so long. The fix was SNI, standardized in 2003: an extension that lets the browser mention the website’s name at the very start of the TLS handshake. In other words, a Host header, reinvented inside TLS. The parallel universe never needs it.

And it’s all on one port. Firewalls, proxies and load balancers deal with port 80 and nothing else. A URL is a URL.

It has been revealed that so if SNI was standardized in 2003, why couldn’t a website rely on it until the mid-2010s? This is the part I find most interesting.

In our universe, TLS is a black box. Your application hands a socket to a TLS library, and the library takes care of everything: negotiating versions, swapping certificates, exchanging keys and the encryption itself. The box comes with a large “do not touch” sign, which is good advice. People who write their own cryptography tend to get it wrong.

According to recent reports, the trouble is that a black box that does everything can only be improved by whoever owns it. Browsers couldn’t use SNI until their TLS library supported it, and on many platforms that library was part of the operating system. Internet Explorer on Windows XP never got SNI at all. A website couldn’t rely on SNI until XP was finally gone.

In the parallel universe, the black box is much smaller. Finding the certificate, checking it and exchanging keys all happen in HTTP, in code that browsers and web servers already update all the time. What’s left inside the box is the genuinely hard part: given these keys, encrypt and authenticate everything that follows. That still deserves a “do not touch” sign, but it’s a box that rarely needs touching. The bits people keep wanting to change live outside it.

The parallel universe’s first request can do another job, too: it makes life much easier for upcoming certificate authorities.

In our universe, a server sends one certificate chain to everyone, before it knows anything about who’s asking. In practice, that means a server operator can only use a CA that every browser on Earth already trusts. Nobody will pick a CA with less than 100% support, however good it is, so a new CA can’t get started. Even Let’s Encrypt, which had about the most compelling offer imaginable (free certificates, issued automatically), had to launch with a cross-signature from IdenTrust, an established CA, so that older browsers would accept its certificates. When that old IdenTrust root expired in 2021, devices that had never learned to trust Let’s Encrypt directly started failing.

In the parallel universe, the browser simply says which CAs it trusts, in the request:.

Sources indicate that the server can hold certificates from several CAs and pick one the browser will accept. That’s content negotiation, which HTTP has done since the beginning. A newly introduced CA can start out with only the newest browsers, and sites can use it alongside their old CA until everyone catches up.

It’s worth noting that a list of trusted CAs, sent in the clear, is one more thing a website could use to fingerprint its visitors. I’d be surprised if it told them much, though. For most people, the list would be whatever came with their browser and operating system, which the User-Agent header already gives away. The exception would be anyone whose employer has added its own root CA to their machine, whose list would announce exactly where they work.

Early implementations in the parallel universe might simply have sent the entire list. As trust stores grew, browsers would probably have evolved more efficient ways to express the same information: compact identifiers, Bloom-filter-style summaries, or a two-stage negotiation where the browser sends a reduced list and the server replies, “I don’t have certificates for any of those authorities, but I do have these.” HTTP has had a status code for exactly that answer since the 1990s: 300 Multiple Choices. At that point the browser can make a second request with a CA it knows is acceptable to both sides.

Our universe is, once again, getting there slowly. TLS 1.3 has an extension that lets a browser list the CAs it trusts, but no browser sends it, partly because a full list is so large. There’s now a proposal called Trust Anchor Identifiers that would let browsers say the same thing in a compact form, so that servers can pick the right certificate. It’s still a draft. And just like SNI, it will only be usable once the TLS library in every browser, operating system and server has caught up.

Recent findings suggest that there’s another secure protocol that was born in 1995: SSH. Look at how it works and it’s already halfway into the parallel universe. An SSH connection opens with both sides exchanging version strings and lists of supported algorithms in the clear, then exchanging keys, and only then switching over to encrypted packets.

According to recent reports, so in the parallel universe, someone at the standards meeting would notice that the TLS people and the SSH people are building the same thing. Both have a handshake that ends with “here are our keys”. Both then need the same thing after that: chop the data into records, number them, encrypt them, authenticate them, and notice if anything is replayed, reordered or dropped. Why have two committees writing two versions of the hardest part?

In a recent development, I think the two groups would merge and settle on a common core. TLS would keep its handshake, with certificates and CAs and an HTTP Upgrade. SSH would keep its own, with host keys you’re asked to trust the first time you connect. Each would finish by handing a set of keys to the same small, heavily-reviewed piece of code. Every improvement to that core, whether a faster cipher or a fix for a subtle attack, would land in both protocols at once.

Recent findings suggest that remember the small black box from earlier? This is where it ends up. HTTP owns the TLS handshake. SSH owns its own. That doesn’t make the handshake easy. Checking a certificate chain is still code where one wrong line can undo everything, as Apple found in 2014 when a single duplicated line skipped the signature check in its TLS handshake. But the handshake lives alongside the rest of the protocol, where it can be reviewed and updated by the same people, on the same schedule. Something like SNI ships with the next browser update, not the next operating system.

In a recent development, the real “do not touch” sign hangs on the shared core that both protocols hand their keys to. It would still be free software, in the GNU sense: anyone can read it, study it, fork it and change it. But the official version would be maintained by cryptographers, and getting a change accepted into it would mean convincing them. Instead of every secure protocol carrying its own significant black box, there’s one small one, with the strictest gatekeepers, and everyone uses it.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t as far-fetched as it sounds. QUIC, the protocol underneath HTTP/3, already works this way. It borrows the TLS 1.3 handshake and nothing else: once the handshake produces keys, they are handed to QUIC’s own packet encryption, and TLS’s record layer is never used. The handshake and the core have already come apart. Our universe just took until 2021 to do it.

There’s a warning in our universe too. In 2023, an attack called Terrapin indicated that an attacker could quietly delete messages from the start of the encrypted part of an SSH connection. It worked by slipping extra messages into the plaintext handshake, which threw off the message numbering the encryption relied on, without either side noticing. The handover from “talking in the clear” to “talking securely” is exactly where the parallel universe would need to be most careful. It’s also exactly the sort of thing you’d want one shared core and one set of eyes on, rather than two.

In a recent development, once the two protocols share a core, the wall between them starts to look a bit thin. In a universe where every secure connection already starts with an HTTP Upgrade, it’s a short step to one more. Sooner or later, someone would modify OpenSSH to accept a shell over HTTP.

That request is sent after the connection has already been upgraded to TLS, so it’s encrypted, and the server knows exactly who’s asking, because the browser (or the SSH client) presented a certificate during the handshake. The server replies 101 Switching Protocols, and what follows is SSH, with its channels, port forwarding and all. TLS has already done the encryption and checked both sides’ identities, so SSH can skip its own key exchange and get straight to the shell. In our universe, WebSocket had to be invented to tunnel things through HTTP. The parallel universe just asks.

Port 22 would still have its fans. Plain SSH doesn’t depend on a CA, so nobody else’s mistake can let an attacker pretend to be your server, and nothing breaks because a certificate expired over the weekend. I expect it would live on in the corner of the server room, run by people who know exactly why they want it.

I’d be a poor advocate if I didn’t look at the downsides, and there’s one big one: stripping.

It has been revealed that credit where it’s due: having https:// as a separate URL scheme does give our real universe something genuinely useful. It’s an explicit sign that security is expected, and that the browser shouldn’t proceed without it. When you click on an https:// link, the author of that page is telling your browser “this must be encrypted, and if it isn’t, stop”.

The parallel universe gives that up. Its security is opportunistic: the browser asks whether the server can do encryption and uses it if so. That’s great, right up until someone hides the opportunity before the handshake completes. The negotiation happens in the clear, so an attacker sitting in the middle doesn’t need to break the encryption. They just stop it from ever starting. Anyone who has set up STARTTLS for email will recognize this one.

So what’s a browser to do? You connect to your bank’s website, ask for /.well-known/tls-cert, and get back “404 Not Found”. Maybe the bank really has forgotten to set up its certificate. Maybe someone in the coffee shop is lying to you. The browser can’t tell the difference. Does it keep going without security?

In fairness, our universe has the same problem. When you type bank.example into your browser, it has traditionally tried plain HTTP on port 80 first. The bank’s server replies with a redirect to https://, and an attacker can simply hide that redirect and keep you on the insecure version. A tool called sslstrip demonstrated exactly that in 2009. Our universe’s answer, for many years, was to train users to look for the padlock.

The parallel universe would end up in much the same place. The padlock would survive as the sign that security was correctly established, and owners would be trained to look for it just as ours were. (Our universe has since turned the padlock inside out. Chrome retired it in 2023, but plain HTTP pages have carried a big “Not Secure” warning since 2018. These days the sign that a connection is secure is that the warning isn’t there.).

Sooner or later, something like HSTS would be introduced, a header the server sends to say “from now on, never talk to me without encryption”. In our universe, HSTS arrived in 2012. In the parallel universe, with no s in the URL to fall back on, I suspect it would have been needed much sooner.

Recent findings suggest that here’s a twist. The parallel universe might end up inventing https:// anyway, but with a different meaning. It wouldn’t mean “use a different protocol on a different port”. It would mean “do HTTP on port 80 as normal, but this time, stop if security can’t be negotiated”. A link author could once again promise that a page must be encrypted, and the bank’s 404 becomes an error page instead of a shrug.

Recent findings suggest that our universe has even written the mirror image of this down. RFC 8164 (2017) describes “opportunistic security” for plain http:// URLs, where a browser can quietly use TLS if the server offers it, while https:// keeps its meaning of “secure or nothing”. Both universes end up with https:// making the same promise. They just got there from opposite ends.

There’s an old argument that the parallel universe would replay, from the other side.

Before Let’s Encrypt arrived in 2015 and made certificates free, a few people ran their servers with self-signed certificates, vouched for by nobody but themselves. Browsers greeted those servers with big scary here-be-dragons warnings. The people running them hated this, and they had a point: a website with no security at all got no warning at all. The browser was treating “encrypted, but I can’t tell who by” as worse than “not encrypted”.

In the parallel universe, the same struggle would happen in a different way. Connect to a site for the first time, with no https:// in the link and no HSTS history, and the opportunistic security kicks in. If the certificate checks out, you get the padlock. If it doesn’t, there’s no padlock, but there’s no need for a warning either. An unknown certificate is much the same as no security at all, and the browser treats it that way.

According to recent reports, going to the effort of TLS without verifying the certificate sounds a bit pointless, but it isn’t entirely. It won’t stop an attacker who can sit in the middle and hand you a certificate of their own. It does stop anyone who can only listen, which is the cheaper and far more common kind of snooping. The IETF came round to this view in 2014, declaring that pervasive monitoring is an attack (RFC 7258) and describing opportunistic encryption as “some protection most of the time” (RFC 7435).

And if you know the magic spell to get into the experts-only configuration, you’ve got the basis for SSH-style security. Tell your browser to remember that certificate, and complain loudly if it ever changes. The first connection is a leap of faith, and every connection after that is checked against it. Our universe’s browsers half-did this already: Firefox had a “Permanently store this exception” checkbox, buried behind enough scary warnings that only the determined ever found it.

Industry observers note that is that a good thing? Depends how you feel about SSH.

In a recent development, here’s the funny thing. Our universe keeps quietly doing it the HTTP way anyway.

Not every lesson points my way, though. Email went the parallel-universe route with STARTTLS, upgrading a plain connection on the normal port. In 2018, RFC 8314 recommended that email clients use a dedicated port with TLS from the very first byte instead, because of the stripping problem.

So was Netscape lazy, or right?

Sources indicate that I think the honest answer is “right for the wrong reasons”, and the parallel universe shows which part was right. The thing that protects you from an attacker quietly downgrading your connection isn’t the separate port. It’s the s in the URL: a promise, made in advance, that this connection must be secure. Netscape almost certainly didn’t choose a new scheme for that reason. A new scheme and a new port were simply the easiest way to bolt encryption onto software that already existed. But the scheme is the part that earned its keep.

The port, I’m less sure about. I can’t help noticing how much of the past thirty years of TLS work has been spent rebuilding, inside a black box, things HTTP already had. I’d have liked to visit the universe where the s in https:// means “this must be secure” and everything else is just HTTP.

SEC Enforcement Staff Examine NVIDIA Accounting, Reuters Reports

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

  • In a recent development, we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Stated It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

In a recent development, we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Industry observers note that each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Sources indicate that then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

It has been revealed that we call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

Sources indicate that we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Industry observers note that table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Industry observers note that training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

Industry observers note that what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

Recent findings suggest that in a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

In a recent development, thinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

In a recent development, if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 demonstrates which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

Industry observers note that the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

It has been revealed that after training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

In a recent development, the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

In a recent development, the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

It has been revealed that figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Sources indicate that pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Recent findings suggest that table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

Industry observers note that these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Sources indicate that selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

It has been revealed that every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

According to recent reports, for the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each enhancement generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

According to recent reports, zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

According to recent reports, no ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

In a recent development, thinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

Sources indicate that we used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

Industry observers note that so we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

In a recent development, figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

Industry observers note that we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Industry observers note that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO upgrade.

It has been revealed that figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Recent findings suggest that nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

MIT Framework Keeps AI Models of Chaos Within Physical Bounds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MIT researchers have developed a machine-learning framework that guarantees bounded trajectories for AI models of chaotic systems, addressing simulations that can drift into physically impossible values during long runs.
  • Sources indicate that the research by graduate student Sunbochen Tang and professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis concerns models of weather, climate, turbulence and other nonlinear processes.
  • Chaotic systems are highly sensitive to initial conditions, so tiny differences can produce dramatically different outcomes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MIT researchers have developed a machine-learning framework that guarantees bounded trajectories for AI models of chaotic systems, addressing simulations that can drift into physically impossible values during long runs. MIT announced the work on November 20, 2026.

Sources indicate that the research by graduate student Sunbochen Tang and professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis concerns models of weather, climate, turbulence and other nonlinear processes. Their paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences was published online on October 12, 2026, and appeared in the journal’s October 20, 2026, issue.

Chaotic systems are highly sensitive to initial conditions, so tiny differences can produce dramatically different outcomes. A neural network may match data over a short period and still fail when left to run: small errors can accumulate until its simulated values grow without limit, even though the real system remains bounded. That behavior can invalidate estimates of long-term statistics, a central goal of modeling dissipative chaotic systems.

The guarantee therefore concerns long-term bounded behavior rather than exact point-by-point forecasting far into the future. It seeks to preserve valid long-run statistics without suppressing the complicated variation that makes the system chaotic. As Azizan put it, “Chaos does not mean anything can happen. These systems often remain bounded, and their models should, too.”.

The framework simultaneously learns a dynamics emulator, which predicts how the system evolves, and an energy-like representation. That representation is used to construct an algebraic dissipative constraint inside a projection layer, which adjusts the model’s predicted evolution. Outside a learned boundary, the energy-like quantity must decrease, drawing trajectories toward the bounded region while allowing chaotic behavior within it.

The paper states this construction enforces dissipation by design and provides formal trajectory-boundedness guarantees over arbitrarily long forecast windows. The learned energy boundary also supplies an outer estimate of the system’s strange attractor, whose complex geometry makes it difficult to characterize directly.

Tang said soft penalties or incentives applied during training need not hold when a deployed model faces upcoming inputs, so unbounded predictions remain possible. Arbitrary caps can keep outputs within a chosen limit, but they can also restrict the model’s ability to represent complex features that should be learned from data. The projection layer is modular and model-agnostic, allowing it to work with different neural-network architectures.

It has been revealed that MIT reports that the approach closely tracked true outcomes in tests ranging from textbook systems to complex multidimensional cases, while conventional methods moved into impossible predictions. The published demonstrations include Lorenz 96 and a reduced-order model of the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation, where the method produced bounded long-horizon forecasts that preserved invariant statistics.

A related Energy-Constrained Operator paper by Andrea Goertzen, Tang and Azizan was published on June 7, 2026. It introduced a closed-form quadratic projection layer and reported stable long-horizon forecasts that captured invariant statistics for systems governed by the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky and Navier–Stokes equations. Both papers use control-theoretic energy conditions to tackle predictions whose unbounded growth prevents meaningful evaluation of long-run statistics.

In a recent development, the algorithms and computer code have been deposited on GitHub, and the paper and open-source code are accessible online. The researchers hope other teams will build on the modular layer and test it on larger, more complex problems.

It has been revealed that the team intends to test progressively larger systems and data-driven models of realistic weather. Realistic-weather performance therefore remains an open research question: the immediate contribution is a formal limit on runaway simulations, while the next tests must establish how that guarantee affects the usefulness of models’ long-term statistics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

According to recent reports, we've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...].

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

Note: you can avoid this step in the future by logging into your LWN account.

Breaking: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package).
  • The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

Recent findings suggest that to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We proposal to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script releases its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

Industry observers note that A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel proposal use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space demonstrates comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Industry observers note that each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

Anthropic declared on November 20, 2026 that it had closed a 1.127 billion-share Class A initial public offering at $83 per share, including underwriters’ full exercise of an option to buy 147 million additional shares. The IPO produced approximately $93.5 billion in aggregate gross proceeds before underwriting discounts, commissions and other offering expenses.

The final offering comprised 1,103,351,354 shares sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 sold by certain selling stockholders. Approximately $91.6 billion of the gross proceeds went to Anthropic, which received no proceeds from the stockholders’ sales.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic’s November 18, 2026 pricing announcement had covered 980 million shares, including 956,351,354 from the firm, and granted underwriters a 30-day option for the additional shares. The selling-stockholder allocation remained unchanged when the option was exercised, so the full exercise expanded only Anthropic’s portion of the offering.

It has been revealed that the final prospectus put the original offering’s aggregate price at $81.34 billion and stated that underwriters would receive no discount or commission on shares sold through the option. The higher final gross figure therefore reflects the additional shares rather than a change in the offering price.

Industry observers note that alongside the IPO, Anthropic closed the sale of 313,253,007 Class N shares at the same $83 per-share price to Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, NVIDIA and TSMC Partners. The private placement had an aggregate purchase price of approximately $26.0 billion. Together, the IPO—including the selling-stockholder shares—and the placement generated approximately $119.5 billion in aggregate gross proceeds before underwriting discounts, commissions and other offering expenses.

Recent findings suggest that the prospectus describes Class N holders as primarily strategic business partners. Each Class A share carries one vote, while Class N shares have no voting rights except where required by law. Class N shares generally convert into Class A when sold or transferred to an unaffiliated third party; Class A shares are not convertible.

It has been revealed that the Class N sale was an unregistered private placement, and underwriters received no discounts or commissions on those shares. The placement shares were not subject to underwriter lock-up agreements, but they were restricted securities that could be resold only under an effective registration statement or an available exemption.

Industry observers note that anthropic’s Class A shares began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on November 19, 2026. Official Nasdaq market data recorded a November 20 regular-session close of $88.91, down $8.26, or 8.50%, from the prior session’s $97.17 close. The session low was $83.05, just above the $83 offering price, leaving the stock above its IPO terms despite the day’s decline.

According to recent reports, the completed transactions give Anthropic substantial fresh capital and place nonvoting Class N shares with seven technology investors. Public Class A holders have a different position: their shares carry voting rights, but their value now moves with the market rather than the fixed IPO terms, as the second-session decline demonstrated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Grafana 13.3 Adds Shared Dashboard Variables and Notebooks.

Nov 21, 2026 2 min read.

Grafana Labs has released Grafana 13.3 with cross-dashboard variables that let teams manage shared dashboard controls in one place. The release also introduces Notebooks for collecting panels and investigation notes in a document that colleagues can share.

In a recent development, the release announcement describes cross-dashboard variables as a public preview across all Grafana editions. Teams can define a variable once and use it in multiple dashboards, avoiding separate configurations for a selector such as an environment or a region. Grafana indicates managing those copies separately can lead to configuration drift.

Cross-dashboard variables address a longstanding user request. In a 2021 GitHub discussion, Grafana user Darth-Bobo described having to maintain the same variables separately across dashboards, warning that configuration differences could become "unmanageable over time". More recently, an early tester described shared variables as useful for evaluating Git Sync without Terraform templating.

According to recent reports, variables can have global scope, which makes them available throughout a Grafana organisation, or folder scope, which limits them to dashboards in the same folder. An editor can add the available variables from a dashboard sidebar, either individually or all at once. Viewers can still change the selected value on a dashboard, while the variable configuration remains centrally managed.

Teams running Grafana themselves must enable the grafana.dashboardGlobalVariables feature toggle to try the preview. Grafana places the management screen under Dashboards > Variables, separate from the dashboard editor where people add the shared controls.

Recent findings suggest that notebooks are also in public preview across all editions. A notebook can hold panels from dashboards or Explore alongside written observations, with findings from Grafana Assistant included as well. Teams can use the document to record how they investigated an issue or to prepare a post-incident review with relevant panels already in place.

Industry observers note that users can create a notebook manually or through Grafana Assistant, then save and share it. Grafana is rolling the feature out gradually to Grafana Cloud. Self-managed installations need the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle enabled.

Grafana’s Notebooks joins similar investigation-document workflows from other observability vendors. Datadog Notebooks combines live graphs with rich text and supports simultaneous editing, inline comments and reusable postmortem templates. New Relic Notebooks, generally available since August 2026, combines NRQL queries, visualisations and Markdown, with natural-language query translation and notebook-wide variables.

Industry observers note that the release also changes how Grafana Assistant builds dashboards. In public preview, dashboard intends let a user describe what they want to monitor and review a proposed layout in chat before building it. The strategy covers the title and the proposed panels, including visualisation types and variables. A read-only preview lets the user refine the plan before choosing to build and save the dashboard.

Sources indicate that A separate Assistant feature, Undo turn, is generally available across all editions. It restores the previous dashboard state after an Assistant edit, including when one request changed multiple panels. The Assistant dashboarding guide notes that undo is unavailable if the dashboard has changed since the Assistant's edit.

Grafana 13.3 also previews a visual refresh with revised themes and interface components. Grafana Labs notes the visual refresh preserves existing navigation and workflows and introduces no breaking changes for plugins. Plugins using standard Grafana components and theme tokens pick up the fresh appearance; those with custom styling can migrate separately. Self-managed people can enable grafana.visualDesignRefresh to try it and switch back to the previous design.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that bloomberg reported on November 20, 2026, that CrowdStrike was in ongoing talks to acquire Zscaler, citing people familiar with the matter, in a report carried by CNBC. Zscaler shares rose 18% in extended trading following the report, while CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%.

No acquisition agreement has been declared. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report, and Zscaler did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

CNBC put CrowdStrike’s market capitalization at $235 billion after its stock roughly doubled during 2026, while Zscaler’s was about $32 billion after a 13% decline during the year.

Sources indicate that A completed transaction would rank among cybersecurity’s largest, CNBC noted. Its comparisons were Google’s $32 billion acquisition of Wiz in 2025, Cisco’s roughly $28 billion purchase of Splunk in 2024 and Palo Alto Networks’ $25 billion acquisition of CyberArk in 2026.

According to recent reports, zscaler’s September 2, 2026 partnership announcement details an existing technical relationship between the companies. The expanded partnership is intended to automate security workflows and support real-time, adaptive Zero Trust enforcement by connecting CrowdStrike’s detection and response with Zscaler’s access controls.

It has been revealed that zscaler mentioned a planned integration using the OpenID Shared Signals Framework, an industry-standard method for sharing risk context, would let Falcon continuously evaluate user risk and pass that context to Zscaler’s Adaptive Access Engine. When suspicious endpoint behavior is detected, Zscaler can then automatically adjust access to match the current risk posture.

The companies are also developing a native Falcon Foundry application built on Zscaler OneAPI. Planned functions include triggering Zscaler enforcement from Charlotte Agentic SOAR, CrowdStrike’s security automation interface, and supporting end-to-end automated remediation without middleware, connectors or separate infrastructure.

Zscaler noted network-event and AI-event logs are designed to stream into Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, CrowdStrike’s security-event management platform, where they can be correlated with Falcon endpoint, identity and cloud data. The combined telemetry is designed to help analysts reconstruct multi-stage attacks across domains. The AI telemetry includes AI-application interactions, risky chatbot prompts and policy violations, placing AI-specific risks alongside network and user activity in a unified investigation interface.

It has been revealed that under the partnership plan, CrowdStrike would also expand Project QuiltWorks, an industry coalition focused on frontier AI risk, to include Zscaler. Zscaler cautioned that unreleased services and features covered by the announcement remained in development and subject to change.

On November 3, 2026, CrowdStrike declared a definitive agreement to acquire Fiddler AI to add pre-deployment evaluation, continuous agent observability and explainability to Falcon. A separate agreement to acquire Dreadnode would add automated pre-deployment security testing of AI models, applications and agents. Both proposed acquisitions were expected to close in CrowdStrike’s fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, subject to customary closing conditions.

According to recent reports, the reported talks sit on top of an existing integration roadmap rather than a relationship built from scratch. The open question is whether that roadmap remains a partner integration or becomes part of a single company; for now, the documented product work and the reported transaction are at different stages, with several of the partnership’s features still in development.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite ↗ Open Full Page

AWS Routes HyperPod Inference Across Regions From One Endpoint

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS introduced Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway on November 20, 2026, giving customers one managed endpoint for inference requests across registered HyperPod clusters in a single AWS Region or multiple Regions.
  • The launch adds a second routing tier above the existing SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway.
  • Industry observers note that AWS is addressing a capacity-utilization problem: requests can queue on a saturated cluster while already-provisioned GPUs sit idle elsewhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AWS introduced Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway on November 20, 2026, giving customers one managed endpoint for inference requests across registered HyperPod clusters in a single AWS Region or multiple Regions. The service selects a cluster using capacity, queue, proximity and error signals, with automatic failover when a cluster becomes unavailable.

The launch adds a second routing tier above the existing SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway. That cluster-level gateway continues to select individual model pods using signals including key-value (KV) cache utilization and queue depth; the fresh global tier selects the cluster first, while leaving pod selection unchanged.

Industry observers note that AWS is addressing a capacity-utilization problem: requests can queue on a saturated cluster while already-provisioned GPUs sit idle elsewhere. In its example of four models served across five clusters in two Regions, per-model serving requires clients to track 20 endpoints. Cluster-level gateways cut that to five, while the global gateway provides one. The managed tier removes the need to build and maintain load balancers, DNS and cross-Region networking for this routing, and lets peak traffic overflow to clusters with available capacity.

An operator publishes each participating cluster by enabling spec.globalRouting in its existing InferenceGatewayConfig, then calls CreateGlobalInferenceGateway with the clusters to group. Publishing creates a Network Load Balancer, a virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint service and certificate resources in the customer’s account. An unpublished cluster cannot be added successfully.

Clients send OpenAI-compatible requests signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) to the regional endpoint. The gateway authenticates the caller and selects a healthy cluster, AWS PrivateLink carries the request within or across Regions, and the cluster’s Inference Gateway chooses the model pod. SageMaker operates the routing fleet, private endpoints, certificate validation, health checks, authentication and rate limiting; a service-managed publisher on each cluster supplies load metrics.

For each request, the gateway scores healthy clusters using four configurable signals:.

Industry observers note that customers overriding the defaults must set all four weights, using values from 0.0 to 1.0 that total 1.0, and can disable a signal with zero. UpdateGlobalInferenceGateway changes the weighting for newly introduced requests without reprovisioning, while in-flight requests finish under the old settings. AWS indicates workloads that prioritize resilience over proximity can raise ErrorRate and lower RegionProximity.

According to recent reports, the gateway health-checks every cluster and shifts traffic to the next-best cluster after a failure without requiring client changes, bringing a recovered cluster back gradually. A failed request is retried once on another cluster unless streaming has started; if no healthy cluster remains, the gateway returns HTTP 503. Adding a healthy cluster does not change the endpoint or disrupt other clusters, while removing one stops fresh requests but lets in-flight work finish.

IAM separately controls standard and streaming invocation, and customer JSON Web Tokens, when used, travel inside the SigV4 signature. Requests reach clusters only over AWS PrivateLink, and AWS states that the gateway does not log or store prompts or completions. Deleting the global gateway stops its endpoint but leaves the per-cluster endpoints serving.

Bagelcode VP of AI Platform Jinhyung Park mentioned in AWS’s announcement that beta tests routed requests across two Regions through the gateway and continued serving them when one cluster could no longer serve the model. That gave the firm’s small platform team cross-Region failover without building or maintaining its own routing layer.

The service is available in 13 Regions: US East (N. Virginia and Ohio), US West (N. California and Oregon), South America (São Paulo), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, London and Stockholm), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo, Mumbai, Singapore and Sydney).

AWS advises single-cluster users to remain on the cluster Inference Gateway endpoint and adopt the global service when adding a second cluster. Existing per-cluster endpoints continue serving during client migration, and a gateway containing only clusters in one Region can keep a workload there. A published cluster left outside any gateway receives no traffic even though its Network Load Balancer continues to run and incur charges.

By putting proximity, capacity and failure signals in one policy, the service makes the use of otherwise idle GPU capacity a configuration decision rather than a separate networking project.

Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • According to recent reports, LFM2 revealed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

According to recent reports, LFM2 revealed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

Industry observers note that the payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

According to recent reports, every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two upcoming in-house encoders:.

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Recent findings suggest that reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a upcoming in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Recent findings suggest that reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

Industry observers note that for brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

It has been revealed that we adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Lambda Now Runs GPU Inference with 48 Concurrent Invocations Sharing One Model per GPU.

Nov 22, 2026 4 min read.

AWS has added GPU support to AWS Lambda: Event Functions running on Lambda Managed Instances can now run on EC2 G-series instances (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f and G6e at launch), deployed as container images, and triggered by the same event sources as any other function. The feature is generally available in the commercial regions where both Managed Instances and G-series instances exist. It is priced at the EC2 On-Demand rate plus a 9.75 percent management fee and the standard $0.20 per million requests.

As InfoQ reported last December, Managed Instances let a function run on EC2 capacity the customer selects and pays for, with Lambda handling provisioning, patching and scaling and several invocations sharing one execution environment. GPUs were missing at that launch. Daniel Abib, senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, describes the operator's side of the change:.

Sources indicate that you build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate.

A capacity provider lists the allowed instance types, the VPC and a vCPU ceiling; Lambda picks the newest generation with capacity and falls back to older generations when newer ones are short:.

The function declares its GPU memory through a new AcceleratorConfig block, next to memory, timeout, storage, and a per-environment concurrency:.

It has been revealed that concurrent invocations in one environment share a single copy of the model in GPU memory, up to 48 per environment, and scaling follows GPU utilization, CPU utilization, and concurrency. Publishing a version provisions the environments, downloads the weights, and warms the engine before the first event arrives; Seekable OCI lazy loading can cut environment start time by up to 70 percent.

AWS ships five GPU base images: CUDA only, CuPy, PyTorch, vLLM, and SGLang. The two inference servers need no handler code; a MODEL_ID variable points to a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an S3 prefix, or a local path, and a model swap is a configuration change followed by a upcoming version:.

It has been revealed that the limits are in the launch post: container images up to 32 GB, 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2 to 32 GB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider, and a timeout of up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations. Abib draws the line against the competition in one sentence: serverless GPU services that hide the same work "often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.".

The first hands-on reports came within a day. Classmethod's Akaike, who had corrected a conference talk in December after finding that no G-type was accepted, tried every accelerated instance type in us-east-1 and found 37 of 81 accepted, all G-family; P-family, G7, Inferentia, Trainium, and the Graviton-based g5g were refused, as were zip packages. A PyTorch benchmark ran about 66 times faster on the L4 than on the instance's CPU. Still, neither Terraform nor the Cloud Control provider knew AcceleratorConfig yet, and the GPU vCPU quota in a fresh account is zero: "if you use g6.xlarge (4 vCPU) with the default three instances, you need a quota of 12 vCPUs." A Terraform provider problem and pull request, opened on 16 November by a user named sasidhar-aws, and a pull request from the same user remain open.

A second test, by an AWS Community Builder writing as xbill, put Gemma 4 E2B on a single g6.2xlarge through the vLLM image, with Google's 4-bit QAT weights and a speculative-decoding drafter baked into a 9 GB image. One environment served all 48 simultaneous requests and every one of 417 calls succeeded, at roughly 130 tokens a second for a single request and 3,400 to 3,600 at 48. The friction was in the pipeline rather than the GPU: 484 seconds from publish to an active version, a Docker image index that Lambda rejected until it was pushed as a single-platform manifest, and a handler that returns complete replies, so time to first token could not be measured. His verdict keeps to that scope:.

Industry observers note that for a model behind events, queues or other AWS services, the Lambda GPU function is the simpler road: one image, one function, and Lambda keeps the server alive and routes the requests. Keep the drafter on for a chat with a few customers at a time, and publish without it for heavy batch load.

When streamed replies or full control of the server are needed, he writes, "run vLLM on an EC2 G6 yourself.".

The pricing model is the one Managed Instances introduced, with a lower fee for GPUs than the 15 percent charged on CPU instance types. Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply to the instance, and there is no duration charge, so an instance bills for as long as the minimum environment count is above zero. Yan Cui's December analysis of the model, written when it still carried the line "GPU instances are NOT supported," applies to the GPU case unchanged:.

Sources indicate that regular Lambda functions can scale rapidly by tapping into a large, shared pool of EC2 instances. With managed instances, it takes tens of seconds to launch upcoming EC2 instances. As such, it's not a good fit when you have large, unpredictable spikes in traffic.

Managed Instances still support only Event Functions, so the GPU path does not yet reach Web Functions, the HTTP-server shape Lambda gained this year, and AWS has not stated whether it will.
