AWS Adds Managed Cluster Extensions to SageMaker HyperPod Slurm

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Web Services launched managed cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm on November 20, 2026, bringing declarative configuration to software on running nodes through APIs or the SageMaker AI console.
  • The launch addresses the part of a shared AI training cluster that changes after provisioning.
  • Administrators can install, configure, enhancement and remove the AWS-managed packages through the console, AWS CLI or an SDK.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Web Services launched managed cluster extensions for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm on November 20, 2026, bringing declarative configuration to software on running nodes through APIs or the SageMaker AI console. The first two extensions cover observability and user management, including directory integration.

The launch addresses the part of a shared AI training cluster that changes after provisioning. HyperPod had already added API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based node setup, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management and deep health checks during 2026. Those features manage the cluster’s definition, capacity, network layout and hardware health; cluster extensions apply the same approach to node software that changes as research teams, monitoring requirements and package versions evolve.

Administrators can install, configure, enhancement and remove the AWS-managed packages through the console, AWS CLI or an SDK. HyperPod validates settings against the selected extension version’s schema before rollout and records the requested version and settings as the desired state. A node agent then applies only the components required by each node’s role, including on nodes added through scaling or replacement.

Updates submit only the settings being changed. HyperPod merges them into the stored configuration and restarts only affected components, without replacing nodes or rerunning lifecycle scripts. New extension versions can also be installed without an AMI patch. HyperPod checks the stored settings against the new version’s schema before rollout, and upgrades only move forward.

Industry observers note that each extension reports Creating or Updating during rollout, Active when every node runs the requested configuration without a reported problem, and Degraded when nodes fail or report problems. DescribeClusterExtension groups node-level health issues by cause with a code, message and affected-node count. HyperPod retries internal failures; administrators can correct other causes and retry affected nodes with an update call containing no configuration changes.

Sources indicate that the sagemaker-observability extension collects node, GPU, Elastic Fabric Adapter, Slurm job and Slurm cluster metrics, sending them to Amazon CloudWatch or Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus. Metric categories, levels and collection intervals are configurable, while nodes run only role-relevant components, such as DCGM and EFA exporters on GPU nodes and Slurm cluster metrics on the controller.

An optional Amazon Managed Grafana workspace adds pre-created Clusters and Jobs dashboards. They connect cluster-wide health and Slurm state with per-node infrastructure metrics and resource use for individual jobs, including CPU, memory, GPU utilization, disk I/O and NCCL data.

The sagemaker-user-management extension creates Linux owners and groups with consistent IDs across nodes, controls SSH and passwordless sudo access by node type, and registers users with Slurm accounting. Accounts can be declared locally, drawn from Active Directory over LDAPS, or both, including connections to AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory. Fresh and replacement nodes receive the same configuration, and administrators can review access through the API instead of signing into each node.

Sources indicate that cluster extensions require a HyperPod Slurm cluster using the November 2, 2026 HyperPod AMI or later, with continuous provisioning enabled. Because extensions run software as root, AWS treats create, enhancement and delete permissions as administrator permissions and advises against granting them to the cluster execution role. That role still needs access to metric destinations and Active Directory secrets, while user management requires a shared file system for home directories. Separate extension ARNs allow platform and monitoring teams to own different extensions.

In a recent development, existing clusters can migrate one capability at a time while scripts and extensions coexist. The process requires updating the cluster software, disabling that capability in lifecycle scripts, manually removing script-installed agents during a maintenance window, and creating the extension on the clean cluster. Each component needs one owner: managing the same exporter, user or service through both mechanisms can cause installation or runtime conflicts. Custom AMIs and lifecycle scripts remain available for organization-specific software, and administrators retain SSH and direct configuration access to every node, including the controller.

Sources indicate that both extensions are available in all Regions where SageMaker HyperPod is supported. There is no additional charge for cluster extensions, but customers pay for underlying resources such as CloudWatch, Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and AWS Secrets Manager.

For shared foundation-model clusters, the operational consequence is that common node software becomes a declared, continuously checked part of cluster state rather than a collection of provisioning scripts. Removing script-installed agents is the one manual fleet-wide migration step; afterward, scale-ups and replacement nodes inherit the same extension settings, while organization-specific tooling remains under the cluster team’s control.

Tech Report: Anysphere Weighs Moving Cursor Away From Chinese Open-Weight Models

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anysphere, the developer of the Cursor AI coding platform, told House investigators it intends to explore phasing out Chinese-developed open-weight AI models because of geopolitical risk, according to a joint congressional report released November 20, 2026.
  • The disclosure is an exploratory initiative, not a completed phase-out, and the committees described no final decision or timetable.
  • Recent findings suggest that open-weight models have trained parameters that can be downloaded, run, and modified independently of the original developer, allowing derivatives to spread without a continuing commercial relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anysphere, the developer of the Cursor AI coding platform, told House investigators it intends to explore phasing out Chinese-developed open-weight AI models because of geopolitical risk, according to a joint congressional report released November 20, 2026.

The disclosure is an exploratory initiative, not a completed phase-out, and the committees described no final decision or timetable. The House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China published the findings after an investigation that began in April 2026 and expanded from Airbnb and Anysphere to DoorDash on July 31, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that open-weight models have trained parameters that can be downloaded, run, and modified independently of the original developer, allowing derivatives to spread without a continuing commercial relationship. The committees stated Composer 2, Cursor’s flagship proprietary model, was built on a Moonshot AI base whose identity became public only after an independent developer identified it.

Sources indicate that cursor’s technical report identifies that base as Kimi K2.5. Composer 2 underwent continued pretraining on a code-heavy data mix, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning in realistic Cursor sessions using the same tools and harness as the deployed model.

According to recent reports, airbnb reported that customized versions of Alibaba’s Qwen models support an AI assistant handling roughly 80,000 guest and host interactions daily, alongside a fine-tuned model summarizing roughly 250,000 support cases and calls each day. Both run on U.S.-based service-provider infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that doorDash reported 25 Chinese model families authorized and deployed in a non-trivial manner, defined as incurring at least $5,000 in computing and serving costs. It estimated that replacing one Chinese-developed model embedded in a larger system could take up to six months, although most other uses could transition almost immediately.

The committees identified cost, customization, and near-frontier performance as adoption drivers, and found that the United States lacks a competitive open-weight alternative at the price and performance the market demands.

The report compares published API prices for one million input tokens and one million output tokens (small pieces of words and characters used to measure model usage):.

Those figures do not adjust for differences in capability, caching, batch discounts, promotions, or self-hosting costs. They illustrate the price pressure behind adoption, while open weights also let companies fine-tune models on their own data and deploy them on infrastructure they control.

Sources indicate that the security concern is separate from hosting location. Running models on U.S. infrastructure reduces direct data exposure, but the report claims that does not change how the underlying model was trained or how it may behave under conditions ordinary evaluations miss.

In a recent development, the report’s 12 recommendations do not themselves enact restrictions. They would build on a Department of Homeland Security order excluding DeepSeek products and services from federal civilian procurement and requiring their removal from agency systems, including third-party products built on DeepSeek. The chairmen recommend extending those restrictions to other Chinese-developed models and their derivatives across federal information systems and federal contract work, with narrow waivers for research, testing, and defensive security. They also recommend barring those models and derivatives from narrowly defined high-risk critical-infrastructure functions, with removal schedules tied to trusted alternatives and temporary exceptions where no trusted substitute exists.

To make the rules enforceable, a model-provenance standard led by the National Institute of Standards and Technology and a machine-readable AI bill of materials would document base models, significant fine-tuning, and distillation sources. The requirement would cover federal contractors and AI used in high-risk critical-infrastructure functions, and would be voluntary elsewhere. A national American open-weight AI initiative would combine public computing resources, shared evaluation infrastructure, voluntary licensing of American frontier-model outputs to qualified open-weight developers for training, and federal anchor demand.

The committees warn that removing Chinese models before trusted open-weight alternatives exist could raise costs and concentrate the market among closed proprietary providers. Anysphere’s exploratory plan therefore illustrates the larger implementation test: restrictions need reliable lineage records to locate embedded models and credible substitutes to avoid trading Chinese open weights for higher costs or closed-model dependence.

Google unveiled on November 21, 2026 that it is providing the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur (IIT Kharagpur) with $5 million to support advanced AI research, expand AI education and build AI capacity across the university’s campus.

Sources indicate that the funding is designed for university researchers and students across three pillars. The research component covers applied AI work in Indic languages, materials science, agriculture and educational technology. The education component supports AI training and curriculum development for students, faculty and teachers.

The capacity-building component will support IIT Kharagpur’s AI frameworks and tooling to strengthen the technological environment across campus. This structure links the research agenda to curriculum development and the technical resources available to the wider university community.

Google said the fund is intended to support applied research and technological solutions benefiting communities across India and beyond, framing deep collaboration and strong academic leadership as necessary for building AI that works for everyone.

Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google and Alphabet, connected the collaboration to his own experience at the institute: “Looking forward to seeing this collaboration shape the path for the next generation of students, just as IIT Kharagpur shaped my own.”.

Pichai also described India as increasingly at the forefront of innovation and mentioned programs like this would help implement Prime Minister Modi’s vision of AI benefits reaching everyone in India.

The funding follows an existing research relationship. On July 10, 2025, Google declared that it was collaborating with IIT Kharagpur researchers to bring the Google Research-led Amplify Initiative to India. The project was designed to give developers and researchers free access to structured, locally grounded datasets reflecting India’s linguistic and cultural diversity. Its aim is to address gaps in large language models resulting from the limited representation of languages, dialects and cultural context in existing AI training data.

Google Research’s original Amplify explanation, published May 2, 2025, described an open platform built around community data collection, with datasets suitable for model fine-tuning and evaluation. It named IIT Kharagpur as its Indian partner, with a remit to gather and validate local material that an AI model could not generate by itself.

Industry observers note that under the collection process, sector experts enter information about key local complications through privacy-preserving Android and web apps. Regional partners and country research leads then translate the queries and assess their local relevance, coherence and fluency, as well as the collection’s coverage. The approach places local experts and partner institutions at the center of both data creation and review.

Sources indicate that in a September 15, 2026 revision, Google reported that Amplify involved more than 1,600 local experts and 20 universities across four continents, including IIT Kharagpur, contributing 15,000 multimodal data points. Those figures cover the full program, not IIT Kharagpur’s individual contribution.

According to recent reports, the new commitment is broader than the Amplify collaboration: it pairs research in several fields with curriculum development and campus AI tooling. For IIT Kharagpur, that connects the questions being investigated with the training and technical resources needed to pursue them.

#69471. My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%

📅 2026-11-15 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1550 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tymscar ↗ Open Full Page

My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%

📅 2026-11-15 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tymscar

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet.
  • It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time.
  • I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.

I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦.

Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

Recent findings suggest that I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

Sources indicate that so it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.

It has been revealed that the adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Industry observers note that then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast….

It has been revealed that I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.

Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the matter is not the monitor again? But it has to be!

Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:.

So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.

Recent findings suggest that why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!

According to recent reports, when the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.

Recent findings suggest that here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an problem. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.

As you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.

Industry observers note that well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.

In a recent development, I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.

It has been revealed that the problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the issues don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1….

So I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a latest adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!

With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames:.

In a recent development, why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:.

In a recent development, I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.

In a recent development, I think the substantial takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?

See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CNBC reported on November 21, 2026 that Anthropic shares closed their second trading session on November 20, 2026 at $88.91, down 8.5%, as the Nasdaq Composite completed a 10% weekly loss, its worst week since the early Covid market turmoil in 2020. The close left the Claude developer with a fully diluted market capitalization of $1.6 trillion, behind only six U.S. companies.

It has been revealed that official Nasdaq historical quotes show that Anthropic opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17 in its November 19, 2026 debut, a 17% gain from the offer price. The shares traded between $83.05 and $92.56 the following day, giving back much of that initial advance.

Sources indicate that nvidia led the broader retreat. CNBC put its weekly decline at 23%, the stock’s sharpest weekly pullback in 18 years, and said the stock had completed its longest weekly losing streak since 2008. Against that backdrop, Anthropic’s second-session decline pointed to investor skepticism about whether the manufacturer can grow into its valuation.

It has been revealed that the earlier offering was still a milestone for venture capital. The enlarged IPO raised a record $93.5 billion, while technology companies bought an additional $26 billion at the offer price, and the debut initially lifted Anthropic’s market capitalization to $1.8 trillion.

Sources indicate that at that offer price, CNBC put Menlo Ventures and Lightspeed Venture Partners’ holdings at about $25 billion each, while Bessemer Venture Partners held roughly $10 billion. The figures show how large a single listing loomed in the venture industry’s returns.

Industry observers note that menlo partner Matt Murphy told CNBC that the firm had delivered more than $1 billion of returns to each of more than five limited partners. “At the end of the day, that’s really our job, is to get dollars back into foundations and endowments,” Murphy said.

According to recent reports, the windfall also contrasts with a subdued listings market. Drawing on University of Florida emeritus professor Jay Ritter’s IPO dataset, CNBC reported that VC-backed technology-IPO proceeds fell from $73.2 billion in 2021 to about $39 billion in total over the following four years. The dataset records 126 technology IPOs in 2021 and 34 in 2025.

Anthropic’s final prospectus reports $17.0 billion of revenue for the three months ended September 30, 2026, up 1,127% year over year, compared with 382% growth in compute and infrastructure expenses. Revenue was $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023. The company presents the faster revenue growth as evidence of compute efficiency.

The customer figures add another dimension to that growth. The prospectus reports more than 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 in trailing-12-month revenue as of September 30, 2026, including more than 1,900 generating at least $1 million and approximately 250 generating at least $10 million.

Recent findings suggest that the capital requirements are substantial. Anthropic disclosed approximately $900.9 billion of committed spending, substantially all related to compute and infrastructure, including $70.7 billion due in the 12 months following September 30, 2026. Before the IPO, the company had raised $141.1 billion of capital as of that date. Its multi-chip architecture spans AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs and AMD GPUs.

Recent findings suggest that CNBC reported that investors were debating whether Anthropic will trade alongside AI hardware companies because of its dependence on chips, memory and data centers, or separately as the first publicly traded pure-play AI developer. InfoQ Homepage News Google Announces Agent Compute Engine for Secure AI Agent Execution.

Nov 22, 2026 2 min read.

Google recently revealed Agent Compute Engine, a managed service that runs AI agents in isolated microVMs, with checkpointing capabilities to suspend and resume execution environments. The design keeps credentials, API keys, and OAuth refresh tokens outside the agent sandbox, using an external Agent Gateway to authenticate requests and inject the required secrets.

Recent findings suggest that google designed Agent Compute Engine to address three requirements at global scale: keeping sandboxes free of exploitable credentials, even when agents make mistakes; minimizing the cost and latency of resuming idle agents; and preserving persistent workspaces across sessions and operating system updates. The infrastructure team writes:.

Agent Compute Engine achieves this by using copy-on-write memory sharing to run multiple agents on a single operating system template, and pausing idle microVMs via fast checkpoint and restore.

Sources indicate that in the deep dive "Inside Agent Compute Engine," Ramanathan Venkatapathy and Rohit Jnagal, distinguished engineers at Google, describe the service’s architecture, covering microVM isolation, credential management, agent identity, storage, and scheduling at scale. They explain the strict separation between the agent harness and sandbox:.

Recent findings suggest that the orchestration harness (the brain) runs completely outside the execution sandbox (the hands), helping ensure that untrusted guest environments only execute explicit commands dispatched by the harness and stream output back. This boundary establishes a deterministic audit trail correlating every harness-initiated tool call with expected compute activity inside the sandbox.

The architecture supports four main workload categories: interactive consumer and enterprise agents that execute code, browse the web, and perform actions; persistent Linux workspaces for autonomous software engineering; large-scale parallel environments for model evaluation and reinforcement learning; and lightweight, sandboxed execution environments for dynamic logic in Google services.

Venkatapathy and Jnagal also describe how the cloud provider uses the platform internally for Gemini, Gemini for Business, the agentic development platform Antigravity, and model evaluation workloads.

It has been revealed that separately, Google offers Agent Substrate, an open-source, Kubernetes-native runtime for running AI agents in isolated environments. Agent Substrate manages sandbox lifecycles independently of the underlying compute infrastructure, allowing idle agents to be suspended while preserving their state and resuming execution on available workers when needed.

In a recent development, in the article "Google's Agent Compute Engine: A MicroVM Sandbox With No Credentials Inside, and What Google Has Not Shipped Yet," Harel Asaf, AI specialist at Elementor, examines the security architecture, the separation of credentials from agent execution environments, and the gaps between Google's announcement and what is at the moment available. Asaf warns:.

Sources indicate that the deep dive gives no boot time, price or density figure for Agent Compute Engine itself. It says developers will control each environment's image, identity, network access and lifecycle, while Google manages the fleet, and that the service is targeted for preview in the coming months. The numbers in the announcement belong to Agent Substrate.

Google is not the only provider offering managed, isolated execution environments for AI agents, with AWS and Azure providing similar capabilities through Bedrock AgentCore and Foundry Agent Service. However, Google’s approach keeps credentials outside agent sandboxes and injects them through an external gateway.

Google also expanded its agent governance capabilities with centralized identity and policy enforcement: the governance stack includes Agent Gateway for traffic control and policy enforcement, Agent Registry for tracking approved agents and tools, SPIFFE-based Agent Identity for authentication and auditing, and OpenTelemetry-compatible observability for monitoring model calls and tool invocations.

In a recent development, agent Compute Engine is not yet available, and pricing has not been declared. The cloud provider is targeting a preview in the coming months. While Agent Substrate is portable across Kubernetes environments, Agent Compute Engine itself is limited to Google Cloud.
